One of our clients registered its trademark in China well before trouble started and still ended up with a shipment stopped by China Customs. The Chinese lawyer had done what the client requested. Nobody had thought to ask what kind of gloves the client sold.
Over the years, our lawyers have represented companies whose Chinese manufacturers registered their trademarks, claimed ownership of their inventions, copied their products, or refused to return their tooling. We have also helped companies stop counterfeiters and recover their property, and those companies succeeded because they had protected themselves in advance. China has laws protecting trademarks, patents, copyrights, and trade secrets, and those laws can provide effective remedies.
I am not a fan of advice telling companies to register every possible trademark, patent, and copyright. For most businesses, that would waste money. A company buying ordinary products from a supplier’s catalog has very different needs from one giving a manufacturer proprietary technology, valuable designs, and custom tooling. The protections should reflect what the company actually stands to lose and what it would cost to recover. For many companies, the contracts governing their Chinese manufacturing relationships matter as much as any registration.

Registering your trademark in the United States, Europe, Canada, or Australia generally does not give you corresponding rights in Mainland China. Chinese law recognizes certain prior rights and provides ways to challenge bad-faith applications, but those proceedings can be expensive, slow, and uncertain. Registering first is far easier than dislodging someone who got there before you.
Many foreign businesses manufacture products in China solely for export. They have no Chinese customers or distributors and no plans to sell to Chinese consumers, but they still have good reasons to register their trademarks there. Their brands appear on products and packaging, and their manufacturers, sourcing agents, and everyone else involved in production know which marks they use. Someone else obtaining a Chinese registration for one of those marks can create serious problems even when every product is headed for a foreign market.
In a case discussed in How to Protect Your Trademarks as China Manufacturing Declines, an American company’s Chinese manufacturer registered 17 of the company’s trademarks without permission, covering essentially one product and nearly all of its components. It then approached the American company’s customers and offered them the same products at prices 40 percent lower. We developed a workaround involving a trademark registration for a visible component of the product and changes to how the products were branded after arriving in the United States. It worked, but the American company had to change its operations to accommodate a problem it should never have faced.
Export-only manufacturing raises some complicated trademark questions, and whether particular manufacturing or export activities constitute infringing trademark use depends on the facts and Chinese legal standards. For most companies manufacturing branded products in China, I still recommend registering their principal trademarks there, whether or not they ever intend to sell to Chinese consumers.

A separate logo registration may also make sense, especially if the logo has substantial commercial value. Word marks often deserve priority because they generally provide more flexibility when a company changes its logo. A combined word-and-logo registration can be useful, but it does not necessarily provide the same protection as separate registrations.
Companies selling in China should also consider registering Chinese-language versions of their brands. Chinese consumers sometimes give foreign brands their own Chinese names, and those names can become commercially valuable. If the foreign company does not choose and protect a suitable Chinese name, someone else may try to register it. A business manufacturing exclusively for export is in a different position, because registering a Chinese-language mark that nobody uses and that has no realistic connection to the business may accomplish little.
China uses the international Nice Classification system, which divides goods and services into 45 classes, but it also divides many classes into narrower subclasses that affect the practical scope of trademark protection. The glove case at the beginning of this article, which we wrote about in China Trademark Registration: Why U.S. Companies Need More Than a Filing Agent, shows what registering in the wrong class costs. The applicant should be the right company within the business’s corporate structure, not a manufacturer, distributor, sourcing agent, or employee. We have seen companies discover during disputes or acquisitions that their Chinese trademarks were registered in the wrong entity’s name. Correcting an ownership problem after the relationship has deteriorated can be difficult, and harder still when the registered owner refuses to cooperate.

Madrid can be efficient for companies maintaining international portfolios, but a direct Chinese application gives greater control over Chinese subclasses and goods descriptions, which is why we generally recommend direct filing. Mainland China, Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan also have separate trademark systems, and a Mainland China registration does not automatically extend to the other three.

China adopted a substantially revised Trademark Law on June 26, 2026, effective January 1, 2027. The revision cuts the opposition period from three months to two, giving businesses less time to oppose conflicting applications before registration. It strengthens provisions addressing certain bad-faith filings and excessive registrations. It also gives CNIPA authority to initiate cancellation proceedings against trademarks that have gone unused for three consecutive years without justification, subject to the applicable procedures. The revised law does not eliminate legitimate defensive registrations, but businesses should have a sound reason for the protection they seek. Chinese trademark practice recognizes that genuine use on goods manufactured in China solely for export can support a registration against non-use cancellation, provided the company has sufficient evidence. Manufacturing contracts, invoices, dated photographs of marked products, shipping records, and Customs documents can all help establish that use. Much of this evidence is held by the Chinese factory, so companies should obtain copies of production records, invoices, and shipping documents while the relationship is good, rather than trying to recover them after a dispute begins. It also depends on the product’s expected commercial life, filing and maintenance costs, and likely enforcement expenses. A business whose advantage depends on a valuable technical invention may have excellent reasons to obtain Chinese patents, and so may a company whose product has a distinctive design that competitors can easily copy. A company with neither is usually better off spending its money on trademark registration, manufacturer due diligence, and a good supply agreement.

If the contract is silent, Chinese law generally favors the party that did the work. Under Article 8 of China’s Patent Law, unless the parties agree otherwise, the right to apply for a patent on a commissioned invention belongs to the party that completed it. For a jointly developed invention, that right belongs to the parties that completed it together. A foreign company that pays a Chinese factory to develop a product without a written agreement on ownership may find that the factory holds the right to patent the result.
China recognizes three principal types of patents. Invention patents protect technical inventions, including products, processes, and improvements. They undergo substantive examination and last 20 years from filing, subject to any permitted term adjustments. Utility model patents protect technical solutions involving the shape or structure of products. They have a lower inventive threshold than invention patents, undergo a more limited initial examination, and last ten years from filing. Design patents protect a product’s appearance rather than its underlying technical function. Design patents applied for on or after June 1, 2021 last 15 years from filing, and earlier ones last ten.
Design patents are most useful for companies whose products have a distinctive appearance that contributes substantially to their commercial value. A business may have little technical innovation to patent and still have a product design competitors can readily copy. Our article China Design Patents: The Info We Need discusses the information and drawings needed for a Chinese design patent application.
Know the scope and likely defensibility of the patents you obtain. Utility model and design patents do not undergo the same substantive examination as invention patents before grant, and a granted patent can still be invalidated if it fails to satisfy the legal requirements. Owning a patent also does not necessarily give a company freedom to manufacture or sell a product, because an improvement may still fall within an earlier patent owned by somebody else.
China generally requires inventions and designs to be novel in light of earlier public disclosures anywhere in the world. A company that publicly discloses a new product before filing can destroy its ability to obtain valid Chinese patent protection, subject to limited statutory exceptions. Sales, trade shows, websites, crowdfunding campaigns, and anything else that reveals the invention or design can all create problems. A company planning to manufacture a new product should therefore settle its patent strategy before introducing the product publicly or sharing sensitive information without protection.
China recognizes foreign priority rights. A qualifying earlier foreign application can generally support a Chinese priority claim, provided the requirements are satisfied. The Chinese application must be filed within 12 months for inventions and utility models or six months for designs. Companies can also use the Patent Cooperation Treaty to pursue international protection for inventions and utility models. The PCT does not itself grant a Chinese patent, and the Chinese filing procedures and deadlines still matter.
Products developed in China carry one more requirement. Under Article 19 of China’s Patent Law, anyone who wants to file a patent application abroad for an invention or utility model completed in China must first submit it to CNIPA for a confidentiality examination. A company that skips that step cannot obtain a Chinese patent on the invention. This catches companies whose engineering happens at their manufacturer or with Chinese engineers, because the invention may count as completed in China even though the company and its patent lawyers are elsewhere.
Copyright protection generally arises automatically when an original work is created. Under Chinese law and the international treaties China has joined, a foreign business ordinarily does not need to register its copyright in China to obtain protection there. This holds for software, photographs, illustrations, artwork, written materials, music, films, and other creative works. Copyright registration never needs renewal, and for many individually authored works the economic rights generally last for the author’s life plus 50 years. Registration can still be worthwhile, particularly when a company expects it may need to prove ownership or pursue infringement in China.
Two gaming matters covered in China Online Gaming IP show what registration can do. Our firm represented a European video game company that registered its trademarks and copyrights in China before launching its game there. When a Chinese company tried to copy the game, we sent a cease-and-desist letter, and the Chinese company backed down. In the other matter, a well-known American game developer came to us after a Chinese company copied its game’s characters and storyline. The American company had a strong potential infringement claim, but it had not registered its copyrights in China, and the evidentiary difficulties and resulting delays made pursuing the infringement commercially unattractive.
Chinese copyright registration is not a prerequisite to every infringement lawsuit. A copyright owner can establish its rights through original files, creation records, contracts, proof of authorship, and other evidence. The trouble comes when that evidence is incomplete, hard to authenticate, or scattered among employees and contractors. A Chinese copyright certificate can make it easier to establish the identity of the work and provide evidence of claimed ownership, though it does not conclusively settle every ownership question. For commercially valuable software, games, and other digital products likely to be copied in China, registration is often worth the cost, because infringing copies spread quickly and delay is expensive.
Copyright protects original expression. It does not generally give a company exclusive rights to the ideas, functions, manufacturing processes, or business concepts embodied in that expression. A company may own copyright in its product photographs, instruction manuals, packaging artwork, or original software and still have no right to stop competitors from manufacturing a product that performs the same function. Copyright can sometimes overlap with trademark or design patent protection. An original logo may qualify for copyright protection while also functioning as a trademark, and certain artistic features of products may receive copyright protection depending on the work and the legal requirements.
Companies frequently overlook ownership. A foreign business pays a Chinese contractor to develop software, prepare technical drawings, or design packaging, and assumes that paying for the work means it owns the copyright. Under Article 19 of China’s Copyright Law, ownership of a commissioned work is determined by the contract between the parties. If the contract does not clearly address ownership, or there is no contract, the copyright belongs to the party that created the work. Before commissioning valuable creative work, a business should establish in writing who will own it, which rights are being assigned or licensed, and whether the creator can reuse it.
The problem gets more complicated when manufacturers hire subcontractors to develop software or other creative components. A foreign buyer may have paid for the finished product without obtaining all the rights needed to modify it or move production elsewhere. Our article Stop Your IP and Key Information from Leaking When Manufacturing Overseas discusses these ownership and disclosure risks.
A company can have excellent trademark, patent, and copyright registrations and still lose control of valuable intellectual property through poorly drafted manufacturing agreements. Trademark registration does not establish who owns your molds. A patent does not necessarily prevent a manufacturer from using confidential information outside the patent’s scope, and copyright protection does not resolve every dispute over work created during product development. These issues belong in the agreements governing the business relationship. As the patent and copyright ownership rules above show, when those agreements are silent, Chinese law can fill the gaps in favor of the party that did the work.
For companies sharing proprietary designs, technical information, or confidential business information with prospective Chinese manufacturers, a well-drafted NNN Agreement can be useful. NNN stands for non-disclosure, non-use, and non-circumvention. Non-use is especially important because a manufacturer has little reason to disclose your proprietary information to anyone else if it can simply use that information to make competing products itself. An ordinary confidentiality agreement may prohibit disclosure without adequately restricting the manufacturer’s own use.
The agreement should reflect the actual risks of the transaction, including what the manufacturer and its subcontractors may do with the company’s designs, technical files, manufacturing methods, and other protected information. Not every manufacturing transaction requires an NNN Agreement, and a company that gives its manufacturer no designs or technical information has little to protect with one. Our Guide to China NNN Agreements explains when these agreements are useful and what they should cover.
Once the parties begin product development or manufacturing, more contractual provisions are usually necessary. The manufacturing agreement should establish who owns existing designs and other intellectual property and who owns improvements developed during the relationship. It should also say whether the manufacturer can use that intellectual property for other customers and what happens when the relationship ends. These agreements should be drafted with the Chinese legal system and its enforcement procedures in mind. Identifying the correct Chinese legal entity, choosing the right dispute-resolution forum, and establishing workable remedies can make an enormous difference when a dispute arises.
One of our clients paid $80,000 for molds used to manufacture its products in China. Eight months later, when it wanted those molds back, its Chinese factory refused, and the company ended up paying another $200,000 to recover tooling it had already purchased. As we explain in The Guide to Molds and Tooling in International Manufacturing, the company lacked an adequate tooling agreement establishing ownership, permitted use, and the factory’s obligation to return the molds. By the time the dispute arose, the factory controlled the tooling and our client needed it to continue production. A tooling agreement should also address the molds separately from the intellectual property embodied in them, because a company can own a mold without necessarily owning every related patent or design right.
Another client did much better because its manufacturing agreement clearly established ownership of the molds held by its Chinese manufacturer. When that manufacturer refused to return them, we worked with Chinese litigation counsel to bring suit and obtain preservation of the factory’s assets. Within about five days, the Chinese court froze the factory’s bank accounts, and the factory returned the molds the following day. The case is described in How to Sue a Chinese Company.
That result was unusually fast, and I would never promise another client the same outcome. This company had an enforceable agreement, the defendant had assets the court could reach, and the available remedy put immediate financial pressure on the manufacturer. That pressure is one reason we generally prefer Chinese court litigation to arbitration for our clients’ manufacturing agreements. Although asset preservation can also be obtained through Chinese courts in qualifying arbitrations, direct court proceedings are often faster and less expensive in our experience.
For some businesses, the most valuable intellectual property is information they do not want to patent or disclose publicly, such as manufacturing methods, formulas, and technical know-how. China protects trade secrets under its Anti-Unfair Competition Law, but the information must meet the statutory requirements. Among other things, it must not be publicly known, it must have commercial value because it is secret, and the owner must have taken appropriate confidentiality measures. A company claiming that its manufacturing process was stolen should be able to identify the protected information and show what it did to keep it confidential. That can include restricting access, imposing confidentiality obligations, controlling the distribution of documents, and contractually restricting manufacturers and subcontractors.
Patent and trade secret protection involve different risks. Patenting generally requires disclosing the invention in exchange for the possibility of exclusive rights for a limited period. Trade secret protection can continue as long as the information remains secret and satisfies the legal requirements, but it does not ordinarily prevent another company from independently developing the same information or lawfully reverse-engineering a product. For technology that competitors can readily discover by examining the finished product, patent protection may be more useful. Valuable manufacturing know-how that can realistically remain confidential may be better protected as a trade secret.
One of the worst proposed China licensing agreements our lawyers have reviewed would have given a Chinese company exclusive, perpetual, worldwide rights to a foreign company’s intellectual property in exchange for 10 percent of sales proceeds. The Chinese company had no meaningful obligation to generate sales. It could have done nothing with the licensed technology, paid nothing, and still prevented the foreign company from licensing the same rights to anyone else, and the proposed agreement even allowed it to assign its rights. Our lawyers suggested that the Chinese company at least commit to minimum sales. It refused. Our client walked away. We describe the full proposal in China Licensing Agreements: Protecting Your IP and Technology.
Had the foreign company signed that agreement, owning its patents, trademarks, and copyrights would not have rescued it from the terms it had accepted. It needed to preserve its ability to exploit the technology if the licensee failed to perform. Licensing agreements should address the rights granted, territory, duration, payment obligations, performance requirements, sublicensing, ownership of improvements, and termination. I also want to know what happens if the licensee stops paying, misuses the technology, or refuses to return confidential materials, because those are the situations in which the terms of a licensing agreement matter most.
A company confronting infringement needs to decide what it wants to accomplish. Recovering molds requires a different approach from stopping counterfeit sales on an online marketplace, and a shipment detained by China Customs creates different problems from a manufacturer selling products made with a customer’s proprietary technology. China provides several enforcement routes, including online platform complaints, administrative proceedings, court litigation, China Customs measures, and criminal enforcement for qualifying conduct. The right choice depends on the infringement, the available evidence, the other party’s assets, and the urgency of the commercial problem.
For counterfeit goods sold online, a platform complaint may resolve the immediate problem faster than litigation. When infringement involves manufacturing or stored inventory in China, administrative enforcement or court proceedings may work better. China Customs can help companies concerned about infringing products entering or leaving the country. Trademarks, copyrights, and patents can be recorded with Customs, and recordation matters because Customs acts on its own initiative only to protect recorded rights. Without a recordation, the rights holder must identify a suspect shipment itself and apply for its detention. Recordation does not guarantee that Customs will catch infringing goods. Our Guide to China Customs IP Recordation explains the process.
A Canadian coat manufacturer contacted our law firm after China Customs detained a major shipment. The company had sold coats under its brand for years, but another business owned the Chinese trademark registration and was using it to prevent the coats from leaving China. Our client wanted to sue. We examined its legal arguments, but every additional week the shipment sat in Customs created more expense and disruption.
We ultimately negotiated the purchase of the Chinese trademark for a six-figure amount, a story we tell in our China Trademark Registration Guide. The company might have had grounds to challenge the other party’s registration, but pursuing them would have taken time its business did not have. Paying that much for rights it should have secured earlier was painful, but under the circumstances buying the trademark made commercial sense.
Before threatening litigation, businesses should also consider what the alleged infringer controls. A Chinese manufacturer may hold the company’s molds, inventory, or technical files. Sending a demand letter without first considering evidence preservation, asset preservation, and the manufacturer’s likely response can make matters worse. Even a strong infringement claim may not justify years of litigation if the likely recovery is small or the defendant has no assets that can realistically be reached.
Before a client begins manufacturing, I want to understand what intellectual property it owns, what it will give the manufacturer, what that manufacturer is permitted to do with it, and what will happen if the relationship ends badly. I also want to know whether the company could realistically enforce the protections we are discussing. Those questions often reveal that the company needs fewer registrations than it expected, a different contract than it planned to use, or protection for something it had overlooked. It is considerably easier to answer them before a factory has your molds and drawings or somebody else has registered your brand.

This holds for software, photographs, illustrations, artwork, written materials, music, films, and other creative works. Copyright registration never needs renewal, and for many individually authored works the economic rights generally last for the author’s life plus 50 years. Registration can still be worthwhile, particularly when a company expects it may need to prove ownership or pursue infringement in China.

Two Video Game Cases

Two gaming matters covered in China Online Gaming IP show what registration can do. Our firm represented a European video game company that registered its trademarks and copyrights in China before launching its game there. When a Chinese company tried to copy the game, we sent a cease-and-desist letter, and the Chinese company backed down. In the other matter, a well-known American game developer came to us after a Chinese company copied its game’s characters and storyline. The American company had a strong potential infringement claim, but it had not registered its copyrights in China, and the evidentiary difficulties and resulting delays made pursuing the infringement commercially unattractive.

Chinese copyright registration is not a prerequisite to every infringement lawsuit. A copyright owner can establish its rights through original files, creation records, contracts, proof of authorship, and other evidence. The trouble comes when that evidence is incomplete, hard to authenticate, or scattered among employees and contractors. A Chinese copyright certificate can make it easier to establish the identity of the work and provide evidence of claimed ownership, though it does not conclusively settle every ownership question. For commercially valuable software, games, and other digital products likely to be copied in China, registration is often worth the cost, because infringing copies spread quickly and delay is expensive.

What Copyright Protects and Who Owns It

Copyright protects original expression. It does not generally give a company exclusive rights to the ideas, functions, manufacturing processes, or business concepts embodied in that expression. A company may own copyright in its product photographs, instruction manuals, packaging artwork, or original software and still have no right to stop competitors from manufacturing a product that performs the same function. Copyright can sometimes overlap with trademark or design patent protection. An original logo may qualify for copyright protection while also functioning as a trademark, and certain artistic features of products may receive copyright protection depending on the work and the legal requirements.

Companies frequently overlook ownership. A foreign business pays a Chinese contractor to develop software, prepare technical drawings, or design packaging, and assumes that paying for the work means it owns the copyright. Under Article 19 of China’s Copyright Law, ownership of a commissioned work is determined by the contract between the parties. If the contract does not clearly address ownership, or there is no contract, the copyright belongs to the party that created the work. Before commissioning valuable creative work, a business should establish in writing who will own it, which rights are being assigned or licensed, and whether the creator can reuse it.

The problem gets more complicated when manufacturers hire subcontractors to develop software or other creative components. A foreign buyer may have paid for the finished product without obtaining all the rights needed to modify it or move production elsewhere. Our article Stop Your IP and Key Information from Leaking When Manufacturing Overseas discusses these ownership and disclosure risks.

Contracts and Trade Secrets: What Registrations Leave Exposed

A company can have excellent trademark, patent, and copyright registrations and still lose control of valuable intellectual property through poorly drafted manufacturing agreements. Trademark registration does not establish who owns your molds. A patent does not necessarily prevent a manufacturer from using confidential information outside the patent’s scope, and copyright protection does not resolve every dispute over work created during product development. These issues belong in the agreements governing the business relationship. As the patent and copyright ownership rules above show, when those agreements are silent, Chinese law can fill the gaps in favor of the party that did the work.

China NNN Agreements and Manufacturing Contracts

For companies sharing proprietary designs, technical information, or confidential business information with prospective Chinese manufacturers, a well-drafted NNN Agreement can be useful. NNN stands for non-disclosure, non-use, and non-circumvention. Non-use is especially important because a manufacturer has little reason to disclose your proprietary information to anyone else if it can simply use that information to make competing products itself. An ordinary confidentiality agreement may prohibit disclosure without adequately restricting the manufacturer’s own use.

The agreement should reflect the actual risks of the transaction, including what the manufacturer and its subcontractors may do with the company’s designs, technical files, manufacturing methods, and other protected information. Not every manufacturing transaction requires an NNN Agreement, and a company that gives its manufacturer no designs or technical information has little to protect with one. Our Guide to China NNN Agreements explains when these agreements are useful and what they should cover.

Once the parties begin product development or manufacturing, more contractual provisions are usually necessary. The manufacturing agreement should establish who owns existing designs and other intellectual property and who owns improvements developed during the relationship. It should also say whether the manufacturer can use that intellectual property for other customers and what happens when the relationship ends. These agreements should be drafted with the Chinese legal system and its enforcement procedures in mind. Identifying the correct Chinese legal entity, choosing the right dispute-resolution forum, and establishing workable remedies can make an enormous difference when a dispute arises.

The $200,000 Mold Problem

One of our clients paid $80,000 for molds used to manufacture its products in China. Eight months later, when it wanted those molds back, its Chinese factory refused, and the company ended up paying another $200,000 to recover tooling it had already purchased. As we explain in The Guide to Molds and Tooling in International Manufacturing, the company lacked an adequate tooling agreement establishing ownership, permitted use, and the factory’s obligation to return the molds. By the time the dispute arose, the factory controlled the tooling and our client needed it to continue production. A tooling agreement should also address the molds separately from the intellectual property embodied in them, because a company can own a mold without necessarily owning every related patent or design right.

Another client did much better because its manufacturing agreement clearly established ownership of the molds held by its Chinese manufacturer. When that manufacturer refused to return them, we worked with Chinese litigation counsel to bring suit and obtain preservation of the factory’s assets. Within about five days, the Chinese court froze the factory’s bank accounts, and the factory returned the molds the following day. The case is described in How to Sue a Chinese Company.

That result was unusually fast, and I would never promise another client the same outcome. This company had an enforceable agreement, the defendant had assets the court could reach, and the available remedy put immediate financial pressure on the manufacturer. That pressure is one reason we generally prefer Chinese court litigation to arbitration for our clients’ manufacturing agreements. Although asset preservation can also be obtained through Chinese courts in qualifying arbitrations, direct court proceedings are often faster and less expensive in our experience.

Protecting Trade Secrets

For some businesses, the most valuable intellectual property is information they do not want to patent or disclose publicly, such as manufacturing methods, formulas, and technical know-how. China protects trade secrets under its Anti-Unfair Competition Law, but the information must meet the statutory requirements. Among other things, it must not be publicly known, it must have commercial value because it is secret, and the owner must have taken appropriate confidentiality measures. A company claiming that its manufacturing process was stolen should be able to identify the protected information and show what it did to keep it confidential. That can include restricting access, imposing confidentiality obligations, controlling the distribution of documents, and contractually restricting manufacturers and subcontractors.

Patent and trade secret protection involve different risks. Patenting generally requires disclosing the invention in exchange for the possibility of exclusive rights for a limited period. Trade secret protection can continue as long as the information remains secret and satisfies the legal requirements, but it does not ordinarily prevent another company from independently developing the same information or lawfully reverse-engineering a product. For technology that competitors can readily discover by examining the finished product, patent protection may be more useful. Valuable manufacturing know-how that can realistically remain confidential may be better protected as a trade secret.

Licensing Can Put Your IP at Risk

One of the worst proposed China licensing agreements our lawyers have reviewed would have given a Chinese company exclusive, perpetual, worldwide rights to a foreign company’s intellectual property in exchange for 10 percent of sales proceeds. The Chinese company had no meaningful obligation to generate sales. It could have done nothing with the licensed technology, paid nothing, and still prevented the foreign company from licensing the same rights to anyone else, and the proposed agreement even allowed it to assign its rights. Our lawyers suggested that the Chinese company at least commit to minimum sales. It refused. Our client walked away. We describe the full proposal in China Licensing Agreements: Protecting Your IP and Technology.

Had the foreign company signed that agreement, owning its patents, trademarks, and copyrights would not have rescued it from the terms it had accepted. It needed to preserve its ability to exploit the technology if the licensee failed to perform. Licensing agreements should address the rights granted, territory, duration, payment obligations, performance requirements, sublicensing, ownership of improvements, and termination. I also want to know what happens if the licensee stops paying, misuses the technology, or refuses to return confidential materials, because those are the situations in which the terms of a licensing agreement matter most.

Enforcing Intellectual Property Rights in China

A company confronting infringement needs to decide what it wants to accomplish. Recovering molds requires a different approach from stopping counterfeit sales on an online marketplace, and a shipment detained by China Customs creates different problems from a manufacturer selling products made with a customer’s proprietary technology. China provides several enforcement routes, including online platform complaints, administrative proceedings, court litigation, China Customs measures, and criminal enforcement for qualifying conduct. The right choice depends on the infringement, the available evidence, the other party’s assets, and the urgency of the commercial problem.

For counterfeit goods sold online, a platform complaint may resolve the immediate problem faster than litigation. When infringement involves manufacturing or stored inventory in China, administrative enforcement or court proceedings may work better. China Customs can help companies concerned about infringing products entering or leaving the country. Trademarks, copyrights, and patents can be recorded with Customs, and recordation matters because Customs acts on its own initiative only to protect recorded rights. Without a recordation, the rights holder must identify a suspect shipment itself and apply for its detention. Recordation does not guarantee that Customs will catch infringing goods. Our Guide to China Customs IP Recordation explains the process.

When the Best Legal Argument Is Not the Best Business Solution

A Canadian coat manufacturer contacted our law firm after China Customs detained a major shipment. The company had sold coats under its brand for years, but another business owned the Chinese trademark registration and was using it to prevent the coats from leaving China. Our client wanted to sue. We examined its legal arguments, but every additional week the shipment sat in Customs created more expense and disruption.

We ultimately negotiated the purchase of the Chinese trademark for a six-figure amount, a story we tell in our China Trademark Registration Guide. The company might have had grounds to challenge the other party’s registration, but pursuing them would have taken time its business did not have. Paying that much for rights it should have secured earlier was painful, but under the circumstances buying the trademark made commercial sense.

Before threatening litigation, businesses should also consider what the alleged infringer controls. A Chinese manufacturer may hold the company’s molds, inventory, or technical files. Sending a demand letter without first considering evidence preservation, asset preservation, and the manufacturer’s likely response can make matters worse. Even a strong infringement claim may not justify years of litigation if the likely recovery is small or the defendant has no assets that can realistically be reached.

Which China IP Protections Does Your Business Actually Need?

Before a client begins manufacturing, I want to understand what intellectual property it owns, what it will give the manufacturer, what that manufacturer is permitted to do with it, and what will happen if the relationship ends badly. I also want to know whether the company could realistically enforce the protections we are discussing. Those questions often reveal that the company needs fewer registrations than it expected, a different contract than it planned to use, or protection for something it had overlooked. It is considerably easier to answer them before a factory has your molds and drawings or somebody else has registered your brand.

articles.content:
Around twenty years ago, an American company called us because its $2 million order of Christmas tree lights was not going to arrive in the United States until December. For a company selling Christmas lights, December delivery is a disaster. We contacted the Chinese factory, only to learn that the people there had never heard of our client. After speaking with the factory and reviewing Chinese-language documents, we discovered that the American company had unknowingly been dealing through a sourcing agent that owed money to the factory. The factory had stopped production because it had not been paid, and our client had no direct contract with the company actually making its products. The American buyer ended up paying millions more to get its lights delivered in time.
I have told that story for years because the underlying mistake is so common. A company thinks it knows its Chinese manufacturer because it has been doing business with the same people for years. It knows who sends the invoices, who answers the emails, and where to wire the money. What it sometimes doesn’t know is which company actually controls production, who owns the assets, and who will be responsible when something goes wrong. As I explain in our guide to overseas manufacturing due diligence, those are things you need to establish before sending money or committing your business to a supplier. The scandal surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO, Jensen Huang, has brought a much larger and more complicated version of these questions into public view.
On November 12, 2026, Nvidia announced Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO amid revelations of his affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese businesswoman and former executive of Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based purchaser of Nvidia’s advanced computing equipment. American intelligence officials reportedly suspect Alice Huang of having connections to Chinese intelligence. China denies those allegations, and no public proceeding has established that she engaged in espionage or that Jensen Huang was coerced into acting on China’s behalf. Much of the coverage has focused on the affair and its national security implications, but the business relationships surrounding Megaspeed deserve attention too. According to The Washington Post’s investigation, Megaspeed’s assets increased from approximately $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024. A relatively obscure company had become a major purchaser of some of America’s most strategically sensitive technology, yet basic questions remained about who financed and controlled it and where its chips ultimately went.
My longtime friend David Dayton recently wrote an excellent article about the controversy, I Don’t Own a Leather Jacket or Have a Chinese Mistress. David has spent more than 30 years working in China and Southeast Asia, speaks Mandarin and Thai, and understands Chinese business as well as anyone I know. His article examines the leverage China’s business and political system gives the government over companies and individuals. I share many of his concerns, particularly those involving opaque business relationships and the financial pressures facing Chinese manufacturers. Our law firm regularly encounters both problems, usually without the billion-dollar transactions or espionage allegations.
David also points readers to an analysis by Desmond Shum, whose book Red Roulette described the complicated relationships among businesspeople, political figures, and wealth in China. In Alice Huang: The Spy Narrative Misses Her Real Business, Shum suggests Alice Huang may have been operating as a commercial intermediary, or what Chinese businesspeople sometimes call a white glove. A white glove acts on behalf of others while obscuring the identity or interests of the people behind a transaction. Shum traces Huang’s involvement in Chinese investment firms, offshore holding companies, and corporate acquisitions. His theory is that her value may have come from arranging transactions and financing for business interests whose involvement was not readily apparent. I find his analysis plausible, though it remains a theory.
Government investigations have since added important facts. On November 12, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs disclosed that its police and customs authorities had begun investigating Megaspeed and related parties in February 2025 over suspected false declarations involving computer servers. Singapore questioned Alice Huang in June 2025 and held her passport while investigating. In February 2026, it concluded there was insufficient evidence to establish that she had committed the suspected declaration-related offenses. It also determined that she had knowingly provided investigators inaccurate information to minimize her role in Megaspeed. Singapore issued her a stern warning, barred her from returning, and expressly stated that it had not investigated her for espionage.
A subsequent joint statement from the U.S. Departments of Commerce and Justice disclosed that Commerce began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 over possible semiconductor diversion. In May 2025, investigators requested Nvidia’s records concerning sales to Megaspeed. The following month, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, and American officials conducted an on-site end-use check in Singapore. The Justice Department subsequently took the lead in a criminal investigation. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and has retained outside counsel to investigate the allegations concerning its business, and neither government has established that it unlawfully diverted Nvidia chips.
The United States has also tightened its export controls. A Commerce Department rule effective November 19, 2026 addresses certain advanced semiconductor transactions and arrangements through which companies in restricted jurisdictions obtain significant computing capacity from overseas data centers. For covered transactions, the rule calls for due diligence concerning direct and indirect ownership or control by persons in specified restricted jurisdictions.
According to The Wire China’s investigation, Alice Huang served as Megaspeed’s managing director from March to November 2023, when the company’s shares were transferred to another Singapore entity, Swiftdata. Yet Singapore identified her as Megaspeed’s CEO, chairperson, and a key controller during its 2025 investigation, American officials interviewed her as CEO in June 2025, and Megaspeed itself says she did not leave the company until August 2025. Those records were not necessarily misleading, because someone can give up a registered directorship and keep running a business. That is exactly why a company’s registered owners and directors do not always tell you who is making its decisions.
Most foreign companies doing business in China will never encounter anything resembling the Megaspeed investigation. Their problems are far more ordinary. They purchase products, pay deposits, provide technical information, and expect their suppliers to perform. Trouble begins when the company named in the contract is not the company controlling what matters.
My colleague Arlo Kipfer recently wrote about a U.S. company our firm represented that had been buying molded plastic products from what it believed was a single Guangdong manufacturing operation. For nearly two years, everything ran through a Hong Kong company that provided quotations, issued invoices, accepted payments, and described the mainland factory as its own production facility. Then the American buyer found a less expensive supplier and decided to move production. When it asked for its molds back, the Hong Kong company explained that it did not own the factory and had no molds to return. The mainland factory was a separate legal entity with which our client had never contracted, and it claimed ownership of the molds because it had paid the toolmaker to produce them.
Our client had spent substantial money on tooling it could not establish that it owned. The factory holding the molds had signed no agreement with our client, while the Hong Kong company that signed the contract had no control over the molds. That is an especially bad position to be in after deciding to change manufacturers. Hong Kong intermediaries can perform perfectly legitimate and valuable functions, including sales, financing, logistics, and export documentation. But related companies remain legally distinct unless there is a basis for holding one responsible for another’s obligations. You cannot assume that a mainland factory is bound by a contract merely because the Hong Kong intermediary calls it “our factory.” Depending on the transaction, proper protection may require a direct agreement with the factory, a three-party contract, a guarantee, or separate agreements allocating responsibilities among the companies involved.
Our lawyers frequently encounter international manufacturing disputes where the company that signed the agreement has few assets and the company holding the products, molds, or technical information never agreed to return them. Sometimes the legal claims are strong enough to pursue. Other times we have to tell the client that litigation would probably cost more than it could realistically recover. That is a terrible conversation to have with a business owner who believed a signed contract meant the company was protected.
A manufacturer that controls the assets your business needs can have enormous leverage even when your contracts identify the correct company. A recent example involved an American company whose Chinese factory demanded an immediate 34% price increase. The factory held the company’s molds and designs and had access to its customer information. Two years earlier, the buyer had signed a single agreement that mixed manufacturing, NNN, and tooling provisions together. When our lawyers reviewed it, they found overlapping provisions and unclear remedies. We advised against suing to recover the molds because the contract was too muddled and obtaining useful relief was too uncertain. We recommended making replacement molds as quickly as possible. Unfortunately, the new molds took longer than expected, and the resulting production shutdown nearly bankrupted the company. I discuss that matter in China Manufacturing Contracts: When One Agreement Is Not Enough.
The factory’s power came from its possession of assets the buyer needed to keep operating. Even if the customer believed it had a valid legal claim, it could not afford to wait months for a resolution while its business was falling apart. I have seen companies spend a great deal of time negotiating contractual protections that look impressive on paper while giving surprisingly little attention to whether they can actually enforce those protections against a manufacturer that refuses to cooperate.
Another client came to us after telling its Chinese manufacturer it wanted to add a second factory to accommodate increased demand. The manufacturer responded by claiming ownership of the Chinese trademarks and patents covering our client’s products. It threatened to seek injunctions against any other Chinese factory that attempted to manufacture or export those products. Six lawsuits later, the parties reached a settlement. What troubles me most about that case is that the American company had not threatened to leave China or reduce its orders. It simply wanted more manufacturing capacity. I wrote about that dispute in How to Negotiate Lower China Manufacturing Prices Without Putting Your Business at Risk.
Some Chinese manufacturers respond constructively when a buyer asks for lower prices or additional production capacity. Others react aggressively to requests the buyer considers entirely reasonable. Sometimes the factory has a legitimate contractual position. Sometimes it is using whatever legal or practical leverage it possesses to protect its business, including claims that ultimately prove difficult to sustain. Before advising a client to negotiate aggressively with an existing manufacturer, I want to know what that factory controls, what rights it can credibly assert, and how much damage it can cause if negotiations go badly. A company that thinks it is strengthening its bargaining position by threatening to move production may instead be warning its supplier to secure whatever leverage it has left.
A manufacturer can perform beautifully for fifteen years and become a serious problem in year sixteen. China’s industrial overcapacity and intense price competition have placed many manufacturers under substantial financial pressure. An October 2026 analysis by the Mercator Institute for China Studies explains how government support, inexpensive financing, and local protectionism allow some Chinese manufacturers to continue operating with extremely low profits or substantial losses. A factory can offer attractive prices and run a full production schedule on modern equipment while struggling to pay its employees or suppliers. Foreign customers often have little idea how serious those financial problems have become until their manufacturer starts demanding larger deposits, delaying shipments, substituting inferior materials, or refusing to release finished goods.
Not long ago, a Midwest furniture company wired $800,000 to a Chinese manufacturer it had worked with for nearly twenty years. The furniture never arrived. The factory closed, its owner disappeared, and the company was left with little realistic prospect of recovering its money. I described that case in China Manufacturing Risks: When Your Reliable Supplier Stops Being Reliable. That client had not selected an unknown factory based on an attractive website or a suspiciously low quotation. It had been doing business with the same manufacturer for almost two decades. The length of the relationship made the company comfortable, but it did nothing to protect the buyer when the factory failed.
Many financially troubled Chinese manufacturers are doing everything they can to survive in extraordinarily competitive markets. But severe financial pressure can change how a factory behaves, especially when it already controls valuable customer assets. This is why I increasingly recommend investigating the financial condition of existing suppliers rather than reserving due diligence for new ones. A twenty-year relationship tells you something about a manufacturer’s past performance. It does not tell you whether that manufacturer can pay its bills today.
I have given well over 100 speeches on protecting intellectual property when manufacturing overseas, and I start nearly all of them by emphasizing three things: choosing a good manufacturer, having contracts that work in the country where production takes place, and protecting the intellectual property essential to your business. The Nvidia controversy adds another reason to pay close attention to the first two. You need to know who actually controls the companies, money, and assets involved, and you need contracts that reflect those realities.
Start by verifying the actual identity of your Chinese business partner. Establish its registered Chinese legal name and its ownership structure to the extent ascertainable, litigation history, and financial condition. Determine whether it owns or operates the factory it claims to operate, who receives your payments, and whether any sourcing agents or trading companies are involved. If a factory asks you to pay a different company or suddenly changes its bank account, investigate before sending the money. I strongly favor visiting factories and meeting their management before entering substantial manufacturing relationships. But a factory visit does not establish that the people showing you around legally own the business, and corporate registration records do not always tell you who exercises practical control. Factories change ownership, accumulate debt, and lose important customers with little warning to their foreign buyers, so these checks need repeating even for suppliers that have performed well for years.
Your contracts must reflect the actual manufacturing arrangement. If a mainland factory will manufacture your products, hold your tooling, or receive sensitive technical information, the agreements need to address that factory’s responsibilities. The correct structure depends on the transaction and may involve several legal entities. A manufacturing agreement should cover production, quality, pricing, delivery, ownership, termination, and remedies, with dispute-resolution provisions designed around where enforcement will be needed. Be especially careful about pricing provisions. We have seen manufacturers agree to fixed prices while retaining an unrestricted right to reject future purchase orders. When the factory wants more money, it simply refuses to accept additional orders at the agreed price. A pricing provision that does not actually commit the factory to supply products may provide much less protection than the buyer expects.
Protect your tooling, trademarks, and technical information before the factory has them. For companies developing or manufacturing custom products, this often means a China NNN agreement before disclosing sensitive information, followed by manufacturing, product development, and tooling provisions appropriate to the transaction. These agreements serve different purposes. An NNN agreement can restrict unauthorized disclosure, use, and circumvention involving your information, but it does not automatically establish ownership of your molds, register your trademarks, or require the factory to manufacture products at agreed prices. Our China NNN agreement guide explains these distinctions in more detail. I also want clients to maintain complete copies of their designs, specifications, and manufacturing files, and to know exactly where their tooling is stored. If another factory cannot reproduce your product without the current manufacturer’s cooperation, you need to understand that dependency before a dispute starts.
You should also know how you would move production if you had to. Not every company needs two factories simultaneously producing the same products, but a business that depends heavily on one manufacturer should know what replacing that manufacturer would entail. How long would it take to qualify another factory? Could you retrieve your molds? Would you need new tooling? Are your Chinese trademarks registered in your company’s name? Does your current supplier possess technical information or claim rights that could interfere with production elsewhere? Those answers tell you how much practical leverage your supplier has, and they help determine when and how to discuss changes in the relationship. I have seen companies create expensive problems simply by announcing their intention to leave before securing the intellectual property and assets they would need for the move.
These precautions are much easier to negotiate while the manufacturer still wants your business. Once a factory suspects it is losing an important customer, it may become far less willing to clarify ownership, return tooling, or agree to restrictions it previously would have accepted. I want clients to establish those rights when everyone is still getting along, not after the factory has stopped answering emails.
None of this means Chinese manufacturers can ignore a well-drafted contract without consequences. One of our clients had a manufacturing agreement that clearly established its ownership of molds sitting in a Chinese factory. When the client decided to move production, the factory refused to return them. We worked with Chinese litigation counsel to sue the manufacturer and seek an order preserving its assets. Within approximately five days, the Chinese court froze the factory’s bank accounts. The factory released the molds the next day.
I discuss that case in How to Sue a Chinese Company. It was an unusually fast result, and I would never suggest that most Chinese manufacturing disputes end that way. But our client had an agreement written for enforcement in China, the defendant had assets a Chinese court could reach, and the legal remedy put immediate financial pressure on the manufacturer. Those circumstances changed the factory’s calculation. Contrast that with the company whose factory demanded a 34% price increase and whose resulting production shutdown nearly put it out of business. Both companies had signed contracts. Only one had a legal position that allowed it to recover its tooling quickly.
Manufacturing in China still makes excellent commercial sense for many of the companies I advise, and many Chinese suppliers are reliable long-term partners. My concern is with companies that become so comfortable with an existing relationship that they stop paying attention to who controls their money, tooling, products, and intellectual property. They assume their contracts protect them because they have never needed to test those contracts.
The questions about corporate identity and control raised by the Megaspeed investigation also arise in the ordinary manufacturing disputes my firm handles. If you depend on Chinese suppliers, compare the companies named in your contracts with the companies that actually receive your money, manufacture your products, hold your tooling, and possess your technical information. If they don’t match, find out why. You may have a perfectly legitimate arrangement that needs better documentation, or you may discover that the company holding something essential to your business has never agreed to give it back.

A Commerce Department rule effective November 19, 2026 addresses certain advanced semiconductor transactions and arrangements through which companies in restricted jurisdictions obtain significant computing capacity from overseas data centers. Those records were not necessarily misleading, because someone can give up a registered directorship and keep running a business. That is exactly why a company’s registered owners and directors do not always tell you who is making its decisions.

Your Contract May Be with the Wrong Chinese Company

Most foreign companies doing business in China will never encounter anything resembling the Megaspeed investigation. Their problems are far more ordinary. They purchase products, pay deposits, provide technical information, and expect their suppliers to perform. Trouble begins when the company named in the contract is not the company controlling what matters.

My colleague Arlo Kipfer recently wrote about a U.S. company our firm represented that had been buying molded plastic products from what it believed was a single Guangdong manufacturing operation. For nearly two years, everything ran through a Hong Kong company that provided quotations, issued invoices, accepted payments, and described the mainland factory as its own production facility. Then the American buyer found a less expensive supplier and decided to move production. When it asked for its molds back, the Hong Kong company explained that it did not own the factory and had no molds to return. The mainland factory was a separate legal entity with which our client had never contracted, and it claimed ownership of the molds because it had paid the toolmaker to produce them.

Our client had spent substantial money on tooling it could not establish that it owned. The factory holding the molds had signed no agreement with our client, while the Hong Kong company that signed the contract had no control over the molds. That is an especially bad position to be in after deciding to change manufacturers. Hong Kong intermediaries can perform perfectly legitimate and valuable functions, including sales, financing, logistics, and export documentation. But related companies remain legally distinct unless there is a basis for holding one responsible for another’s obligations. You cannot assume that a mainland factory is bound by a contract merely because the Hong Kong intermediary calls it “our factory.” Depending on the transaction, proper protection may require a direct agreement with the factory, a three-party contract, a guarantee, or separate agreements allocating responsibilities among the companies involved.

Our lawyers frequently encounter international manufacturing disputes where the company that signed the agreement has few assets and the company holding the products, molds, or technical information never agreed to return them. Sometimes the legal claims are strong enough to pursue. Other times we have to tell the client that litigation would probably cost more than it could realistically recover. That is a terrible conversation to have with a business owner who believed a signed contract meant the company was protected.

How Chinese Manufacturers Gain Leverage Over Their Customers

A manufacturer that controls the assets your business needs can have enormous leverage even when your contracts identify the correct company. A recent example involved an American company whose Chinese factory demanded an immediate 34% price increase. The factory held the company’s molds and designs and had access to its customer information. Two years earlier, the buyer had signed a single agreement that mixed manufacturing, NNN, and tooling provisions together. When our lawyers reviewed it, they found overlapping provisions and unclear remedies. We advised against suing to recover the molds because the contract was too muddled and obtaining useful relief was too uncertain. We recommended making replacement molds as quickly as possible. Unfortunately, the new molds took longer than expected, and the resulting production shutdown nearly bankrupted the company. I discuss that matter in China Manufacturing Contracts: When One Agreement Is Not Enough.

The factory’s power came from its possession of assets the buyer needed to keep operating. Even if the customer believed it had a valid legal claim, it could not afford to wait months for a resolution while its business was falling apart. I have seen companies spend a great deal of time negotiating contractual protections that look impressive on paper while giving surprisingly little attention to whether they can actually enforce those protections against a manufacturer that refuses to cooperate.

Another client came to us after telling its Chinese manufacturer it wanted to add a second factory to accommodate increased demand. The manufacturer responded by claiming ownership of the Chinese trademarks and patents covering our client’s products. It threatened to seek injunctions against any other Chinese factory that attempted to manufacture or export those products. Six lawsuits later, the parties reached a settlement. What troubles me most about that case is that the American company had not threatened to leave China or reduce its orders. It simply wanted more manufacturing capacity. I wrote about that dispute in How to Negotiate Lower China Manufacturing Prices Without Putting Your Business at Risk.

Some Chinese manufacturers respond constructively when a buyer asks for lower prices or additional production capacity. Others react aggressively to requests the buyer considers entirely reasonable. Sometimes the factory has a legitimate contractual position. Sometimes it is using whatever legal or practical leverage it possesses to protect its business, including claims that ultimately prove difficult to sustain. Before advising a client to negotiate aggressively with an existing manufacturer, I want to know what that factory controls, what rights it can credibly assert, and how much damage it can cause if negotiations go badly. A company that thinks it is strengthening its bargaining position by threatening to move production may instead be warning its supplier to secure whatever leverage it has left.

China’s Economic Problems Make These Risks Worse

A manufacturer can perform beautifully for fifteen years and become a serious problem in year sixteen. China’s industrial overcapacity and intense price competition have placed many manufacturers under substantial financial pressure. An October 2026 analysis by the Mercator Institute for China Studies explains how government support, inexpensive financing, and local protectionism allow some Chinese manufacturers to continue operating with extremely low profits or substantial losses. A factory can offer attractive prices and run a full production schedule on modern equipment while struggling to pay its employees or suppliers. Foreign customers often have little idea how serious those financial problems have become until their manufacturer starts demanding larger deposits, delaying shipments, substituting inferior materials, or refusing to release finished goods.

Not long ago, a Midwest furniture company wired $800,000 to a Chinese manufacturer it had worked with for nearly twenty years. The furniture never arrived. The factory closed, its owner disappeared, and the company was left with little realistic prospect of recovering its money. I described that case in China Manufacturing Risks: When Your Reliable Supplier Stops Being Reliable. That client had not selected an unknown factory based on an attractive website or a suspiciously low quotation. It had been doing business with the same manufacturer for almost two decades. The length of the relationship made the company comfortable, but it did nothing to protect the buyer when the factory failed.

Many financially troubled Chinese manufacturers are doing everything they can to survive in extraordinarily competitive markets. But severe financial pressure can change how a factory behaves, especially when it already controls valuable customer assets. This is why I increasingly recommend investigating the financial condition of existing suppliers rather than reserving due diligence for new ones. A twenty-year relationship tells you something about a manufacturer’s past performance. It does not tell you whether that manufacturer can pay its bills today.

Protect Your Business Before the Relationship Deteriorates

I have given well over 100 speeches on protecting intellectual property when manufacturing overseas, and I start nearly all of them by emphasizing three things: choosing a good manufacturer, having contracts that work in the country where production takes place, and protecting the intellectual property essential to your business. The Nvidia controversy adds another reason to pay close attention to the first two. You need to know who actually controls the companies, money, and assets involved, and you need contracts that reflect those realities.

Start by verifying the actual identity of your Chinese business partner. Establish its registered Chinese legal name and its ownership structure to the extent ascertainable, litigation history, and financial condition. Determine whether it owns or operates the factory it claims to operate, who receives your payments, and whether any sourcing agents or trading companies are involved. If a factory asks you to pay a different company or suddenly changes its bank account, investigate before sending the money. I strongly favor visiting factories and meeting their management before entering substantial manufacturing relationships. But a factory visit does not establish that the people showing you around legally own the business, and corporate registration records do not always tell you who exercises practical control. Factories change ownership, accumulate debt, and lose important customers with little warning to their foreign buyers, so these checks need repeating even for suppliers that have performed well for years.

Your contracts must reflect the actual manufacturing arrangement. If a mainland factory will manufacture your products, hold your tooling, or receive sensitive technical information, the agreements need to address that factory’s responsibilities. The correct structure depends on the transaction and may involve several legal entities. A manufacturing agreement should cover production, quality, pricing, delivery, ownership, termination, and remedies, with dispute-resolution provisions designed around where enforcement will be needed. Be especially careful about pricing provisions. We have seen manufacturers agree to fixed prices while retaining an unrestricted right to reject future purchase orders. When the factory wants more money, it simply refuses to accept additional orders at the agreed price. A pricing provision that does not actually commit the factory to supply products may provide much less protection than the buyer expects.

Protect your tooling, trademarks, and technical information before the factory has them. For companies developing or manufacturing custom products, this often means a China NNN agreement before disclosing sensitive information, followed by manufacturing, product development, and tooling provisions appropriate to the transaction. These agreements serve different purposes. An NNN agreement can restrict unauthorized disclosure, use, and circumvention involving your information, but it does not automatically establish ownership of your molds, register your trademarks, or require the factory to manufacture products at agreed prices. Our China NNN agreement guide explains these distinctions in more detail. I also want clients to maintain complete copies of their designs, specifications, and manufacturing files, and to know exactly where their tooling is stored. If another factory cannot reproduce your product without the current manufacturer’s cooperation, you need to understand that dependency before a dispute starts.

You should also know how you would move production if you had to. Not every company needs two factories simultaneously producing the same products, but a business that depends heavily on one manufacturer should know what replacing that manufacturer would entail. How long would it take to qualify another factory? Could you retrieve your molds? Would you need new tooling? Are your Chinese trademarks registered in your company’s name? Does your current supplier possess technical information or claim rights that could interfere with production elsewhere? Those answers tell you how much practical leverage your supplier has, and they help determine when and how to discuss changes in the relationship. I have seen companies create expensive problems simply by announcing their intention to leave before securing the intellectual property and assets they would need for the move.

These precautions are much easier to negotiate while the manufacturer still wants your business. Once a factory suspects it is losing an important customer, it may become far less willing to clarify ownership, return tooling, or agree to restrictions it previously would have accepted. I want clients to establish those rights when everyone is still getting along, not after the factory has stopped answering emails.

What a Good China Contract Can Actually Accomplish

None of this means Chinese manufacturers can ignore a well-drafted contract without consequences. Within approximately five days, the Chinese court froze the factory’s bank accounts. The factory released the molds the next day.

I discuss that case in How to Sue a Chinese Company. It was an unusually fast result, and I would never suggest that most Chinese manufacturing disputes end that way. But our client had an agreement written for enforcement in China, the defendant had assets a Chinese court could reach, and the legal remedy put immediate financial pressure on the manufacturer. Those circumstances changed the factory’s calculation. Contrast that with the company whose factory demanded a 34% price increase and whose resulting production shutdown nearly put it out of business. Both companies had signed contracts. Only one had a legal position that allowed it to recover its tooling quickly.

Manufacturing in China still makes excellent commercial sense for many of the companies I advise, and many Chinese suppliers are reliable long-term partners. My concern is with companies that become so comfortable with an existing relationship that they stop paying attention to who controls their money, tooling, products, and intellectual property. They assume their contracts protect them because they have never needed to test those contracts.

The questions about corporate identity and control raised by the Megaspeed investigation also arise in the ordinary manufacturing disputes my firm handles. If you depend on Chinese suppliers, compare the companies named in your contracts with the companies that actually receive your money, manufacture your products, hold your tooling, and possess your technical information. If they don’t match, find out why. You may have a perfectly legitimate arrangement that needs better documentation, or you may discover that the company holding something essential to your business has never agreed to give it back.
