articles.content:
I recently spoke with a Beijing lawyer friend I have worked with on many cross-border disputes, and he asked how our China manufacturing work was going. “China is totally back,” I told him. During the worst of the U.S.-China tariff battles, companies regularly came to us after trying to find manufacturers in Mexico, Vietnam, or elsewhere. They had concluded that the alternatives could not make their products, could not make them at the required quality or volume, or were too expensive even after accounting for the China tariffs. We hear that story much less now. Most companies contacting us about manufacturing in China have already decided to manufacture there.
He then asked about China Plus One, or China+1, the practice of adding manufacturing or sourcing outside China to reduce dependence on it. I told him we still discuss it about once a month, usually because I raise it. Often the client is already in a dispute with a Chinese manufacturer or with Sinosure, China’s state-owned export credit insurer. At that point I want to know what happens to the company’s business if its Chinese factory stops shipping. The answer may matter more than the legal merits of the dispute.
I have written about China Plus One since 2014, and my advice has changed less than the enthusiasm surrounding the strategy. China remains difficult to replace. A company can have very good reasons to keep manufacturing there and equally good reasons to make sure it has somewhere else to go.
China’s advantage is the industrial system it has spent decades building. In one manufacturing region, a buyer can often find a capable factory, the component suppliers that feed it, the engineers who can fix a design problem, and the tooling shops that can make a replacement part in days. For a complicated product, having all of those people close together saves time and money that may never show up in a factory’s quoted unit price.
This is especially important for small and midsize American importers, whose Chinese manufacturers may handle product development, component sourcing, tooling, packaging, and production. In another country the buyer may have to provide complete engineering files, arrange component supply, and manage far more of the process itself. A factory in Mexico or Vietnam might make an excellent product once the buyer solves those problems, but the cost of getting there can still make the move uneconomic. We have seen businesses spend months exploring alternatives and then decide to keep buying from China. I have no quarrel with that decision. The danger lies in assuming that a good relationship with one factory makes contingency planning unnecessary.
Consider a client we wrote about earlier this year. Its Chinese manufacturer demanded an immediate 34 percent price increase, and the factory had the client’s molds, designs, and customer information. The buyer had signed a single agreement combining its manufacturing, tooling, and confidentiality protections, but the overlapping provisions and unclear remedies left it in a weak position. We advised against suing to recover the molds because, under that contract and in those circumstances, making new molds was likely to be quicker and less expensive. The new molds took longer than expected, production stopped, and the interruption nearly bankrupted the company.
Another American company told its Chinese manufacturer it needed a second factory to meet increased demand. It was not planning to leave China or even cut its purchases from the existing supplier. The factory nevertheless claimed ownership of the Chinese trademarks and patents covering the products and threatened to stop any other Chinese factory from making or exporting them. The parties settled, but only after six lawsuits in four different cities and two countries.
Those cases are why I ask about the buyer’s ability to move production before discussing litigation strategy. I want to know who owns the molds, whether the buyer can actually retrieve them, and whether it has the native design files and specifications. I also want to know whether another factory could make the product and whether an unidentified subcontractor or component supplier has something the buyer cannot readily replace. A favorable judgment several years from now will not fill next month’s customer orders.
Sinosure can make the calculation harder. A buyer that withholds payment over defective goods may find itself facing collection demands from Sinosure or its agents, and the dispute can affect its access to credit from other Chinese suppliers. We have handled more than 100 Sinosure matters, and one of my first questions is how much the company needs to keep sourcing from China. A business with no realistic alternative may need to approach the dispute differently from one that can keep operating elsewhere. Leaving China does not erase a legitimate debt or settle a contract claim, but it can change how dependent the buyer is on the Chinese manufacturing system while the claim is resolved.
A recent AmCham Shanghai article on China Plus One in Thailand features Mark Plum and Alex Bryant of East West Associates, who have spent decades helping companies manufacture in China and Southeast Asia. One of their clients wants to replicate its Suzhou production at a new facility in Rayong, Thailand, making the same product to the same standard in either location and shifting work between them as costs, freight, duties, demand, and capacity change. For a company with the resources to run two plants, that flexibility has real value.
East West Associates describes recent greenfield projects costing $50 million to $100 million and taking roughly 18 to 24 months from the initial decision process to operation. Thailand has a substantial manufacturing base in electronics, automotive components, appliances, and HVAC equipment, and its Board of Investment can offer valuable incentives for qualifying projects. For companies prepared to build and operate a second plant, those advantages deserve attention. Many of our American importer clients are looking for a contract manufacturer, not a second plant, and a company buying $500,000 or $2 million worth of product a year cannot approach China+1 as a $50 million construction project.
AmCham Shanghai’s 2026 China Business Report provides some context. Among its 262 responding member companies, the share redirecting planned China investment to other markets fell to 39 percent, the lowest in several years, and 48 percent of those redirecting investment chose Southeast Asia. Those figures tell us what AmCham Shanghai’s members are doing, and many of them have substantial operations in China. They tell us much less about an American importer looking for a second contract factory.
A well known luxury brand client of ours moved manufacturing from China to Vietnam before COVID and for years told us how much it preferred Vietnam. Then it announced it was planning to move back to China. Its Vietnamese operation still needed components from China, sometimes on short notice because of design changes or inventory problems, and flying those parts in was driving up the costs. I told that story in our earlier discussion of whether companies should leave China.
Another client moved manufacturing from China to Latin America and discovered that it still needed a small spring from China. A spring can be a minor item on the bill of materials and still keep a capable factory from shipping finished product. That is the kind of dependence companies too often seem to find out about after they’ve committed to a new factory.
There is a geopolitical reason to look this closely at components. A disruption involving Taiwan could affect shipping and manufacturing well beyond the Taiwan Strait, and China has used export controls on critical materials, including rare earths, in its trade disputes. On November 9, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce extended the suspension of certain October 2025 export controls through January 10, 2027. But the export licensing requirements imposed on seven rare-earth elements in April 2025 remain in effect. If both of your factories need a critical material that only China can reliably supply, moving final assembly has not solved that risk.
U.S. tariff rules have changed repeatedly in 2026. On February 20, the Supreme Court held in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorize the president to impose tariffs. That decision did not eliminate the longstanding China-specific Section 301 duties or tariffs imposed under other statutes. In July, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative imposed new Section 301 duties on imports from 60 economies over their failure to prohibit or effectively restrict imports made with forced labor.
China itself faces a new 12.5 percent duty on covered products, generally on top of its existing Section 301 tariffs. For a Chinese product already subject to a 25 percent Section 301 tariff, that can mean 37.5 percent in combined Section 301 duties before ordinary customs duties, assuming no applicable exemption. Vietnam and Thailand also face the new 12.5 percent duty on covered products, while Mexico faces 10 percent, with an exemption for goods entered duty-free under the USMCA. There are important product exemptions, including for goods subject to Section 232 tariffs. Those separate tariffs, which cover certain steel, aluminum, and other products, have their own requirements and do not necessarily disappear when manufacturing moves to another country. The point is to calculate the duties on your actual product before assuming that leaving China will save you money.
Country of origin is a separate problem. Shipping finished Chinese goods to Thailand for repackaging does not ordinarily make them Thai goods, though genuine manufacturing in Thailand can change the result, depending on the product and what the factory does. No universal percentage of local content automatically makes every product Thai, Vietnamese, or Mexican. Mexico is more complicated still because a product may have Mexican origin for one customs purpose and fail to qualify for preferential treatment under the USMCA. As we explain in our guide to moving manufacturing from China to Mexico, the USMCA has product-specific requirements, and Chinese inputs can affect whether the finished product qualifies for preferential treatment when it enters the United States. At the July 1, 2026 joint review, the United States declined to renew the USMCA in its existing form, though the agreement remains in force.
The Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act creates another risk for products manufactured outside China when they incorporate covered inputs from Xinjiang or from entities on the UFLPA Entity List. A factory move does not necessarily eliminate that exposure. For an important relocation decision, I would want a customs specialist to determine the proper classification, the applicable origin rules, and the total duties before anyone signs a long-term manufacturing commitment. When the answer is uncertain, U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s binding-ruling process is worth considering.
A company considering China+1 should review its existing Chinese manufacturing relationship before giving anyone else its designs or telling its current factory it might lose business. Start with what you will need to make the product elsewhere. Verify who owns the tooling, whether the contract requires its return, who has the native CAD and other technical files, and whether your factory can legally withhold them. Register and protect important trademarks and other intellectual property in the countries where you manufacture and plan to manufacture. Our articles on China exit planning and IP and protecting IP when manufacturing beyond China explain why this work should come before the supplier learns of your plans.
We have seen what happens when a company gets the timing wrong. In one case we described years ago, a U.S. buyer told its Chinese manufacturer it would be moving production to Mexico and Thailand and then discovered that someone in China had registered its brand names and logos as trademarks in those countries. The company now faced an obstacle to manufacturing under its own brand in the very places it hoped to go. I would rather spend money on trademark searches and filings before the move than on a fight over who has the right to use the brand afterward.
Good contracts also matter when things go wrong. One client’s Chinese manufacturing agreement clearly gave it ownership of the molds at its factory. When the factory refused to release them, we retained Chinese litigation counsel, filed suit, and secured a court order freezing the manufacturer’s bank accounts within about five days. The factory released the molds the next day. We have written about that case and why the contract mattered. The result was unusually quick, and the availability of that remedy depends on the facts and the local court. It is a useful contrast with the company forced to remake its molds after its contract failed to give it a practical path to recovery.
Once a new manufacturer is identified, the legal work continues. The agreement needs to fit the country’s law and the actual production arrangement. The buyer needs clear rights over its designs, tooling, and product-development work, enforceable specifications and quality standards, meaningful restrictions on unauthorized subcontracting, and a sensible way to resolve disputes against the party that actually controls production. A Chinese NNN or manufacturing agreement should not simply be relabeled for use in Thailand or Vietnam. A company building its own factory, rather than hiring a contract manufacturer, also has investment, labor, tax, and environmental requirements to deal with.
Start with the product, not a list of supposedly hot manufacturing countries. Thailand may be an excellent choice for an electronics or appliance maker and Mexico for products sold mainly in North America, but what matters is whether an actual factory can meet your specifications, volume, price, delivery needs, and compliance requirements, using components it can reliably obtain. Count the complete landed cost of the finished product and the expense of managing a second supplier. I see no point in moving production if it means worse products or costs that make your business uncompetitive.
For many smaller businesses, I would begin by qualifying a backup manufacturer without immediately moving a large portion of production. Have it make samples and, where feasible, a trial production run. Verify its legal identity and capabilities, see whether its suppliers can support the product, and establish how long it would take to increase production if the Chinese factory stopped. At the same time, secure the rights and technical information you need to use that backup. Some companies will find that meaningful diversification is too expensive for now. They will at least know their exposure and can decide whether additional inventory, alternative components, or better contracts would reduce it.
I am happy to help a client keep manufacturing in China when China remains its best option. What I do not want is for that client to discover, in the middle of a fight over invoices or molds, that nobody else can make its product and that its current factory knows it.

For a Chinese product already subject to a 25 percent Section 301 tariff, that can mean 37.5 percent in combined Section 301 duties before ordinary customs duties, assuming no applicable exemption. Vietnam and Thailand also face the new 12.5 percent duty on covered products, while Mexico faces 10 percent, with an exemption for goods entered duty-free under the USMCA. There are important product exemptions, including for goods subject to Section 232 tariffs. Those separate tariffs, which cover certain steel, aluminum, and other products, have their own requirements and do not necessarily disappear when manufacturing moves to another country. The point is to calculate the duties on your actual product before assuming that leaving China will save you money.

Country of origin is a separate problem. Shipping finished Chinese goods to Thailand for repackaging does not ordinarily make them Thai goods, though genuine manufacturing in Thailand can change the result, depending on the product and what the factory does. No universal percentage of local content automatically makes every product Thai, Vietnamese, or Mexican. At the July 1, 2026 joint review, the United States declined to renew the USMCA in its existing form, though the agreement remains in force.

The Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act creates another risk for products manufactured outside China when they incorporate covered inputs from Xinjiang or from entities on the UFLPA Entity List. A factory move does not necessarily eliminate that exposure. For an important relocation decision, I would want a customs specialist to determine the proper classification, the applicable origin rules, and the total duties before anyone signs a long-term manufacturing commitment. When the answer is uncertain, U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s binding-ruling process is worth considering.

A company considering China+1 should review its existing Chinese manufacturing relationship before giving anyone else its designs or telling its current factory it might lose business. Start with what you will need to make the product elsewhere. Verify who owns the tooling, whether the contract requires its return, who has the native CAD and other technical files, and whether your factory can legally withhold them. Register and protect important trademarks and other intellectual property in the countries where you manufacture and plan to manufacture. Our articles on China exit planning and IP and protecting IP when manufacturing beyond China explain why this work should come before the supplier learns of your plans.

We have seen what happens when a company gets the timing wrong. In one case we described years ago, a U.S. buyer told its Chinese manufacturer it would be moving production to Mexico and Thailand and then discovered that someone in China had registered its brand names and logos as trademarks in those countries. The company now faced an obstacle to manufacturing under its own brand in the very places it hoped to go. I would rather spend money on trademark searches and filings before the move than on a fight over who has the right to use the brand afterward.

Good contracts also matter when things go wrong. One client’s Chinese manufacturing agreement clearly gave it ownership of the molds at its factory. When the factory refused to release them, we retained Chinese litigation counsel, filed suit, and secured a court order freezing the manufacturer’s bank accounts within about five days. The factory released the molds the next day. We have written about that case and why the contract mattered. The result was unusually quick, and the availability of that remedy depends on the facts and the local court. It is a useful contrast with the company forced to remake its molds after its contract failed to give it a practical path to recovery.

Once a new manufacturer is identified, the legal work continues. The agreement needs to fit the country’s law and the actual production arrangement. The buyer needs clear rights over its designs, tooling, and product-development work, enforceable specifications and quality standards, meaningful restrictions on unauthorized subcontracting, and a sensible way to resolve disputes against the party that actually controls production. A Chinese NNN or manufacturing agreement should not simply be relabeled for use in Thailand or Vietnam. A company building its own factory, rather than hiring a contract manufacturer, also has investment, labor, tax, and environmental requirements to deal with.

What I Recommend to Smaller Importers

Start with the product, not a list of supposedly hot manufacturing countries. Thailand may be an excellent choice for an electronics or appliance maker and Mexico for products sold mainly in North America, but what matters is whether an actual factory can meet your specifications, volume, price, delivery needs, and compliance requirements, using components it can reliably obtain. Count the complete landed cost of the finished product and the expense of managing a second supplier. I see no point in moving production if it means worse products or costs that make your business uncompetitive.

For many smaller businesses, I would begin by qualifying a backup manufacturer without immediately moving a large portion of production. Have it make samples and, where feasible, a trial production run. Verify its legal identity and capabilities, see whether its suppliers can support the product, and establish how long it would take to increase production if the Chinese factory stopped. At the same time, secure the rights and technical information you need to use that backup. Some companies will find that meaningful diversification is too expensive for now. They will at least know their exposure and can decide whether additional inventory, alternative components, or better contracts would reduce it.

I am happy to help a client keep manufacturing in China when China remains its best option. What I do not want is for that client to discover, in the middle of a fight over invoices or molds, that nobody else can make its product and that its current factory knows it.

The factory had stopped production, and our client had to pay millions more to get its lights delivered. A company that can move production easily has options unavailable to one dependent on a single specialized manufacturer. Don’t assume you can move production to Mexico or Vietnam quickly just because you’ve found a factory willing to make your products. In an ideal world, you will have considerable overlap of factories so as to be sure that your new factory is truly capable of getting things right.

We’ve seen manufacturers promise low prices and then fail to deliver, leaving foreign buyers with supply problems and little realistic chance of recovery. We would rather identify those vulnerabilities before negotiations begin.

Others required substantial preparation, including securing IP, resolving disputes, and developing alternative suppliers before the first pricing discussion.
Chinese factories have plenty of ways to retaliate. As I explain in Why Demand Letters to China Suppliers Often Backfire, they can delay your orders, hold your finished goods or tooling hostage, and even try to use your own trademark against you.

The $4,500 fee covers a focused review of existing documents, with the scope agreed upon in advance. We identify significant risks and explain what we recommend doing about them before you begin negotiations. Reviewing each additional set of manufacturing contracts with another supplier costs $1,000, assuming a comparable scope and level of complexity. The audit does not include detailed supplier due diligence or the legal work needed to fix any problems we identify. We will discuss the scope and cost of any additional work with you before proceeding. The goal of these audits is to find and fix problems while you still have options. A missing China trademark registration, an unfavorable ownership arrangement, or a poorly drafted manufacturing agreement might be relatively easy to address while things are going well. It eventually paid another $25,000 to purchase the mold outright, and we drafted a mold ownership agreement that eliminated the continuing surcharge. What began as a seemingly harmless accommodation had turned an $8,000 mold into a nearly one million dollar expense.

If you have a sourcing agent, you should get clear on what you are really paying it before you go to your factory for a lower price.

Those promises create expensive obligations if your business changes or your manufacturer fails to perform.

The company hired a quality-control firm to inspect future production and negotiated a price reduction covering half the inspection cost. That was more useful than demanding a lower unit price and hoping quality would remain acceptable. Any price reduction should be documented in a way that protects the savings negotiated. A lower quoted price is worth little if the factory can refuse future orders, change delivery obligations, or compromise quality. The right agreement depends on your existing contracts, products, and commercial relationship.
If you’re considering negotiating lower prices with your Chinese manufacturer, contact our China legal team before approaching the factory. We can help you identify risks, get your China legal house in order, and pursue the savings without putting your manufacturing operations in jeopardy.

We’ve had Chinese factories respond to requests for lower prices by telling foreign buyers they’re finished manufacturing for them. Some announce that they intend to sell the products themselves. Others just quietly do it.  Depending on the relationship, your factory may have your designs, technical specifications, manufacturing methods, and customer information. It may already be producing similar products for other buyers. If your legal protections are weak, you may be giving your manufacturer an opportunity to become your competitor.

5. A Commercial Dispute Creates Risks for Your People in China

My firm has represented foreign companies dealing with threats of violence, detention, and restrictions on leaving China. Chinese courts and other authorities can impose exit restrictions in certain circumstances involving civil disputes and enforcement proceedings. Official exit bans differ from detention or threats by private parties. When a company has a serious disagreement with a Chinese manufacturer, we generally advise against sending its executives to China to negotiate until we’ve assessed the risks. Having legitimate reasons to withhold payment, demand compensation, or terminate a manufacturing relationship does not necessarily protect your people from an angry counterparty or legal measures that could prevent them from leaving.

What Should Determine Your China Factory Price Negotiating Strategy?

When companies contact us about negotiating lower manufacturing prices, they usually have a number in mind. I want to know that number, but I’m more interested in making sure that their legal and commercial position is well fortified first.

1. What Does Your Manufacturing Contract Say?

One factory demanded a 34 percent price increase, effective immediately, and the U.S. company on the receiving end came to us for help. The factory held the company’s molds, designs, and customer information. Two years earlier, the buyer had signed one agreement combining manufacturing, tooling, and NNN provisions. Overlapping provisions and unclear remedies made it a poor weapon against the factory. We advised the company that suing to recover its molds would probably be slower and more expensive than making new ones. The new molds took longer than expected, and the resulting production shutdown nearly bankrupted the business.

We’ve also had companies come to our law firm believing that they had guaranteed manufacturing prices when their contracts merely listed prices without requiring the factory to accept future orders. When the manufacturer wanted more money, it rejected the next purchase order. A price commitment that doesn’t oblige the factory to supply products is not really a price commitment at all. Your contract’s provisions regarding pricing, orders, termination, intellectual property, tooling, and dispute resolution affect your negotiating position, and so does the identity of the company that signed it. An impressive-looking contract can be nearly worthless if it doesn’t bind the Chinese factory controlling your production and assets.

Many years ago, an American company contacted us after learning that its $2 million order of Christmas tree lights would not be delivered when needed. We called the Chinese factory, which told us it had never heard of our client. It turned out the buyer had unknowingly been dealing through a sourcing agent that owed money to the factory. The factory had stopped production, and our client had to pay millions more to get its lights delivered. The buyer had no direct contract with the factory and little influence over the company making its products.

2. How Strong Are Your Intellectual Property Protections?

Your IP protections determine how much damage a manufacturer can do if negotiations turn hostile. We look at trademark and patent registrations, NNN and manufacturing agreements, ownership of designs and tooling, and whether the appropriate legal entities hold the relevant rights. We also want to know what protections are missing, particularly in countries where the buyer might move production. A company can have a good Chinese trademark registration and still lack effective contractual restrictions preventing its manufacturer from using its designs to compete. Another can have a strong NNN agreement and discover that someone else owns the Chinese trademark for its principal product. We’ve also seen valuable IP rights held by a Chinese subsidiary when they should have been held elsewhere.

Trademark registrations and NNN agreements protect against different problems. A registration provides rights under trademark law, while an NNN agreement creates contractual obligations governing the manufacturer’s use of information and its dealings with the buyer. Companies often need both, but the appropriate protections depend on the products, the relationship, and the rights already secured. Whether additional IP protections are necessary depends on what the company already has and what its manufacturer could do if the relationship deteriorates. We want to know which situation the client is in before the factory has any reason to become uncooperative.

3. What Industry Are You In, and How Dependent Are You on Your Factory?

If you’re buying standard consumer products from an industry with excess capacity, you may have several alternative manufacturers. Your position is different if your products require specialized machinery, unusual materials, difficult-to-obtain certifications, or expertise possessed by only a handful of factories. We also consider how long replacing the manufacturer would take and what an interruption would cost, including whether you have enough inventory to keep supplying customers and whether missed deliveries would cost you major accounts or an entire retail season. A company that can move production easily has options unavailable to one dependent on a single specialized manufacturer. Don’t assume you can move production to Mexico or Vietnam quickly just because you’ve found a factory willing to make your products. In an ideal world, you will have considerable overlap of factories so as to be sure that your new factory is truly capable of getting things right.

4. How Financially Healthy Is Your Manufacturer?

If material costs have declined, a reduction can benefit both parties. If the factory cannot pay its suppliers or employees, an attractive price can be an attempt to postpone collapse. We’ve seen manufacturers promise low prices and then fail to deliver, leaving foreign buyers with supply problems and little realistic chance of recovery. For major manufacturing relationships, we sometimes recommend investigating the manufacturer’s finances, ownership, litigation history, and operating capabilities before making new commitments.

5. What Are Your Financial, Employment, and Corporate Exposures in China?

A price negotiation can also expose unresolved problems elsewhere in your China operations. When companies come to us wanting to secure a price reduction (or leave China entirely), we look at outstanding supplier invoices, disputed deposits, quality claims, and other possible financial obligations. If you have a Chinese subsidiary, joint venture, employees, or other personnel in China, we also consider whether those arrangements create additional risks if the manufacturing relationship deteriorates. A company that buys products from an independent Chinese factory faces different risks from one with employees, assets, and ongoing business operations in China. Employment, tax, and corporate compliance issues do not necessarily involve the manufacturer, but they can become important if a pricing disagreement develops into a broader dispute or decision to leave China. We would rather identify those vulnerabilities before negotiations begin.

Before Negotiating Lower Prices, Get Your China Legal House in Order

Price negotiations can expose legal weaknesses that have gone unnoticed for years. Addressing those weaknesses while the factory relationship is still good can prevent expensive problems. Once a manufacturer believes it is losing a major customer, obtaining its cooperation can become much harder. Another client of ours had the right protections in place. Its manufacturing contract clearly established its ownership of its molds. When the company decided to move production, the Chinese factory nevertheless refused to release them. We worked with Chinese litigation counsel to sue the manufacturer and seek an order preserving its assets. Within about five days, the Chinese court froze the factory’s bank accounts. The factory released the molds the following day.

Most international disputes don’t resolve that quickly, and I’d never promise a similar outcome. But this case shows what a well-drafted, locally enforceable contract can accomplish. We are always happy to try to help a client reduce its China manufacturing costs by 20 percent, but I wouldn’t want to discover that pursuing the reduction put its trademarks, molds, inventory, or production at risk. Before asking for lower prices, make sure you know who owns the assets and intellectual property your manufacturing depends on. Some of our best results have come from straightforward negotiations between businesses that wanted to keep working together. Others required substantial preparation, including securing IP, resolving disputes, and developing alternative suppliers before the first pricing discussion.

Chinese factories have plenty of ways to retaliate. As I explain in Why Demand Letters to China Suppliers Often Backfire, they can delay your orders, hold your finished goods or tooling hostage, and even try to use your own trademark against you.

Our $4,500 China Legal Audit

At Harris Sliwoski, we offer a $4,500 China legal audit to help companies prepare to negotiate lower prices with their Chinese manufacturers or move production out of China entirely. The audit focuses on four areas:

  • Intellectual property. We review your existing China IP protections, who owns the relevant rights, and any significant gaps that could put your trademarks, designs, technology, or other valuable IP at risk.
  • Employment. If you have employees or other personnel in China, we look for employment-related legal issues that could cause problems if you change manufacturers or scale back your China operations.
  • Entity structure. If you have a Chinese subsidiary, joint venture, or other China entity, we review its ownership, control, and potential legal vulnerabilities.
  • Manufacturing contracts. We review one set of manufacturing contracts with one supplier, looking particularly at provisions that could affect your price negotiations, your ability to switch factories, or your ability to leave China.

The $4,500 fee covers a focused review of existing documents, with the scope agreed upon in advance. We identify significant risks and explain what we recommend doing about them before you begin negotiations. Reviewing each additional set of manufacturing contracts with another supplier costs $1,000, assuming a comparable scope and level of complexity. The audit does not include detailed supplier due diligence or the legal work needed to fix any problems we identify. We will discuss the scope and cost of any additional work with you before proceeding. The goal of these audits is to find and fix problems while you still have options. A missing China trademark registration, an unfavorable ownership arrangement, or a poorly drafted manufacturing agreement might be relatively easy to address while things are going well. Once your relationship with your Chinese factory starts falling apart, those same problems can become far more difficult and expensive to resolve.

How to Negotiate Lower Prices Without Losing Your Chinese Manufacturer

Once a client’s legal and commercial position is clear, we can decide how aggressively to negotiate and what approach is most likely to succeed. Before contacting the factory, I also want to know what the company is actually paying for.

Find Out Where Your Money Is Going

A client that began manufacturing in China around 1995 could not afford an $8,000 mold and accepted the factory’s proposal to add $1 to the price of every widget instead. Nearly fifteen years later, a new employee discovered the surcharge was still being collected. By then, the company had paid approximately $850,000 in additional charges. It eventually paid another $25,000 to purchase the mold outright, and we drafted a mold ownership agreement that eliminated the continuing surcharge. What began as a seemingly harmless accommodation had turned an $8,000 mold into a nearly one million dollar expense.

Sourcing agents can also add large, sometimes hidden, costs. We’ve had clients eliminate Chinese sourcing agents and discover their factories would sell directly to them for much less. In one instance, our buyer learned that an agent claiming a 5 percent commission had actually been charging 45 percent and collecting an additional 15 percent from suppliers. If you have a sourcing agent, you should get clear on what you are really paying it before you go to your factory for a lower price.

Give Your Manufacturer a Good Commercial Reason to Reduce Prices

Increased order volumes, more predictable production schedules, lower material costs, or sharing the expense of tariffs can give a manufacturer a commercial reason to cut its prices. The strongest argument can be that the factory has enjoyed a profitable relationship with the buyer for years and should make a concession to preserve it. Some factories agree to deep reductions just to keep a good customer, and others have reduced prices without receiving anything in return. A factory operating at full capacity and turning away business has little reason to cut its prices. Be careful about offering higher purchase volumes, long-term commitments, or other concessions merely to obtain a lower unit price. Those promises create expensive obligations if your business changes or your manufacturer fails to perform.

Don’t Sacrifice Product Quality to Get a Lower Price

A client of ours discovered that approximately 30 percent of the electronic devices shipped by its Chinese manufacturer had obvious defects, including cracked screens and scratched casings. The company hired a quality-control firm to inspect future production and negotiated a price reduction covering half the inspection cost. That was more useful than demanding a lower unit price and hoping quality would remain acceptable. Any price reduction should be documented in a way that protects the savings negotiated. A lower quoted price is worth little if the factory can refuse future orders, change delivery obligations, or compromise quality. The right agreement depends on your existing contracts, products, and commercial relationship.

If you’re considering negotiating lower prices with your Chinese manufacturer, contact our China legal team before approaching the factory. We can help you identify risks, get your China legal house in order, and pursue the savings without putting your manufacturing operations in jeopardy.

articles.content:
My law firm’s China lawyers draft far more distribution agreements than they did a few years ago, and we rarely form Chinese companies for clients anymore. I estimate we helped set up more than 100 Chinese entities from 2005 to 2015 and fewer than ten over the next decade. Foreign companies still want Chinese customers, but many have lost their appetite for putting employees and substantial assets in China. A U.S. furniture manufacturer we represent wanted its American employees out of China, and it ended up selling its China business to the manager who ran it and financing most of the sale. I have favored using Chinese distributors for years, and I have watched Western companies spend a fortune trying to sell good products in China on their own, with disappointing results.
Selling in China is hard, and most of the clichés about doing business there have some truth to them. It is not one market, and you can do well in Shanghai and get nowhere in another city. A capable Chinese distributor knows the customers and has people on the ground to deal with the messiness of selling there, but the wrong one can tie up your market for years while selling almost nothing.
A distributor takes on much of the sales work and, depending on the agreement, after-sales support. The foreign supplier avoids the cost of a Chinese subsidiary and its employment, tax, and administrative obligations. Some of our clients have well-known products in China and no office or employees there. For other ways to reach Chinese customers without setting up a local company, see 6 Smart Strategies for Selling to China Without Being in China.
Using a distributor does not end the foreign supplier’s China obligations. It still has to comply with Chinese product rules and protect its trademarks, and collecting from the distributor is its problem too. For many of our clients, the smaller physical presence is still worth a great deal, and keeping employees out of China also lowers the risk of exit bans arising from commercial disputes.
I start out skeptical of a distributor that approaches you first, because wanting your product says nothing about whether it can sell it. I want to know what a prospective distributor has actually sold, where it has sold it, and who buys from it. “National coverage” often turns out to mean a warehouse and two salespeople, so a company claiming a nationwide network ought to be able to name its salespeople and the customers they cover. Check its ownership and litigation history, and look hard at its finances, including whether it has the money to promote a new product or expects you to pay for the entire launch.
Experience with other foreign suppliers is useful, especially when those relationships have lasted. Ask for references and actually call them. Then ask my favorite question: How does our product fit with what you already sell? A distributor with complementary products can be an excellent choice. If it is making good money selling competing products, look much harder. Good China due diligence catches some of these problems before anyone signs.
Clients often bring us distribution agreements that have worked in Europe, the United States, or Australia. We use them as a starting point because they reflect how the client does business, but we almost always rewrite substantial parts of them for China, and the issues below are where most of that rewriting happens. We cover the questions we ask before drafting in China Distribution Contracts: The Questions We Ask.
The first question is who sells to the Chinese customer. A conventional distributor buys from the foreign supplier and resells on its own account. An agent finds customers and helps arrange sales for the supplier, usually for a commission. Our clients generally prefer the distributor model because the Chinese company takes direct responsibility for local sales and customer payments, and because it makes clear who handles importation.
Chinese law looks beyond what the contract calls the distributor to how the relationship actually works. A distributor that routinely signs contracts on your behalf can create Chinese tax exposure for you. Depending on the structure, the arrangement can also fall under China’s franchise rules, which turn on how the business operates, including the rights the foreign supplier grants and the fees it collects.
I pay close attention to titles and authority. A distributor’s key person often needs a serious title, such as China Director, to get meetings, above all with government buyers. We pair that title with a board-approved authorization letter that spells out exactly what the person can and cannot do on the client’s behalf, for reasons we explain in Setting Up Your Chinese Distributor for Success: Titles and Authority Matter. The agreement needs to say whether the distributor can use sub-distributors and who answers for their conduct. Anti-bribery provisions belong here too. They matter most when the customers include state-owned enterprises or government bodies, and they need to address both Chinese law and, where it applies, the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act.
I have lost count of how many problems began with a foreign company assuming that its U.S. or European trademark registration protected it in China. China is primarily a first-to-file country. A distributor can apply to register your brand, and getting it back can be expensive. When a distributor has registered a client’s mark, we can usually negotiate an assignment if the distributor wants to keep the relationship, and the odds improve when its real money comes from manufacturing the client’s products for export. Refusals tend to come from distributors that do not make the products or that earn more using the brand in China themselves.
A Norwegian company once asked us about suing its former Chinese distributor, which was manufacturing and selling the Norwegian company’s products in China. The company believed it owned the Chinese trademark. After all, the distributor had given it a registration certificate. The certificate was fake. The mark had been registered to a Chinese individual who was licensing it to the former distributor. What the company thought was a straightforward breach-of-contract claim had become a much harder case.
Register the mark in your company’s own name before the distributor starts using your brand. At the very least, get your application on file first, though a pending application is not the equivalent of an issued registration. Choose your Chinese-language brand name yourself. If you leave that decision entirely to your distributor or the market, Chinese customers can end up knowing your product by a name someone else picked. Our China trademark registration guide explains the filing process, and China Trademarks and Your Chinese Distributor covers what a distributor can do to you by filing first.
We give the distributor only the trademark rights it needs to market and sell our client’s products. Those rights end with the distribution agreement, subject to any agreed inventory sell-off rights. The distributor may not register the client’s marks, Chinese names, logos, domains, or confusingly similar brands. Where a registered mark is licensed, we address recordal of the license with the Chinese trademark authorities. An unrecorded license is generally valid between the parties but cannot be asserted against good-faith third parties. If the distributor will receive valuable confidential information, we consider the protections in our China NNN agreement guide.
Before granting distribution rights, we check whether the product needs testing, certification, registration, Chinese labeling, or import permits. The agreement says who obtains and pays for each approval. If the distributor is responsible, we set a deadline and specify the consequences for missing it. Without that, a foreign supplier can wait indefinitely for sales that cannot legally begin.
I always want to know whose name will appear on each approval. An American medical device company we represented let its Chinese distributor act as its registration agent because the distributor offered to handle the paperwork at no charge. Five years later, the company wanted a stronger distributor. The old one was sitting on the registration certificate and the technical file and had no reason to cooperate. Every month it stalled was a month without sales. Where Chinese rules allow, we usually want the registration in our client’s name.
The agreement specifies who handles warranty service and pays for recalls, including whether the supplier warrants directly to end customers or only to the distributor. Those provisions do not automatically shield the manufacturer from Chinese product-liability claims. If the distributor has few assets and inadequate insurance, its promise to indemnify the manufacturer is not worth much after a major product problem.
Chinese distributors often ask for nationwide exclusivity. A distributor that knows the Shanghai market well does not necessarily have useful contacts in Chengdu or Guangzhou, and I rarely like granting rights to all of China without a strong business reason. We define the territory, products, and customers the distributor’s rights cover, and whether our client keeps the right to sell directly or appoint other distributors.
We have seen companies sign five-year exclusive agreements and learn, two or three years in, that the distributor never placed a single order. The distributor signed to keep the product off the market while selling its own competing line, a pattern I describe in International Distribution Agreements: Beware the Eager Distributor. When our clients do grant exclusivity, we normally attach minimum purchase requirements, because purchases show up on invoices and claimed retail sales are much harder to verify. The agreement defines how performance is measured, any cure period, and the consequences of missing a target. During the exclusive period, we generally bar the distributor from handling competing products, after checking that restriction against the competition law that applies.
I like to give the supplier the right to end exclusivity without terminating the agreement. Suppose a distributor is selling a reasonable amount in Shanghai but nowhere near enough to justify control over all of China. Our client can appoint another distributor for the uncovered market and keep the Shanghai relationship if it still makes commercial sense.
Clients worried about heavy discounting sometimes want to require their Chinese distributors to maintain minimum resale prices. We examine Chinese antitrust law before putting such restrictions in a contract. Article 18 of China’s Anti-Monopoly Law restricts agreements that fix resale prices or set minimum resale prices. China’s rules effective February 1, 2026 provide only a narrow safe harbor for certain fixed or minimum resale-price restrictions. In general, the party relying on the safe harbor has to prove that each party had less than a 5% share of its respective relevant market in every year of the agreement and that annual turnover of the covered goods stayed below RMB 100 million. Where the supplier has multiple distributors, their market shares in the same relevant market and the turnover of the covered goods are aggregated. Even if those thresholds are met, the safe harbor does not apply where evidence shows the agreement eliminates or restricts competition.
For most clients, we focus on the supplier’s wholesale price and let the distributor determine its own resale prices. None of our clients has ever had a real resale-price problem in China, but a number of distributors have threatened to sue our clients or report them to the authorities when relationships turned rocky, claiming minimum prices our clients never imposed. The agreements contained no price restrictions to support those threats. When resale price control matters to the business, we review the specific restriction and the law that applies before anyone signs. Form contracts imported from other countries cause enough trouble that we do not rely on whatever price clause the client’s standard agreement contains.
I keep seeing the same fight start before a single order is placed. The supplier assumes the distributor will pay for advertising in exchange for exclusivity. The distributor expects the supplier to fund trade shows and provide samples, translations, and technical support. Nobody has worked out a budget. Six months later, both sides are annoyed, and sales have barely begun.
We try to settle who pays for what before we start drafting. If the distributor promises to translate manuals by a deadline or demonstrate the product to specified customers, we put those obligations in the agreement, along with our client’s marketing commitments. A general promise to “promote the brand” is useless when the first year’s sales come in far below expectations.
For a new distributor, I favor payment before shipment. After I wrote about selling into China without being there, two clients emailed me with the same advice. However you structure the deal, get paid enough up front to make it worth your while, because there is a very good chance you will never see another cent. Once the distributor establishes a payment history, a client may decide to offer 30-day terms. If it does, the agreement needs a way to return to advance payment when the distributor pays late or its finances deteriorate. We often put prices in a separate schedule, with a defined procedure for updating them, rather than locking prices into a long-term contract.
Shipping terms create avoidable disputes when the parties use familiar acronyms without understanding what they require, so identify the Incoterms rule and the named place. For many shipments, FCA (Free Carrier) makes more sense than EXW (Ex Works), which puts export clearance on the buyer even when that buyer is in China. For containerized freight, CIP (Carriage and Insurance Paid To) often fits better than CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight), which was designed for goods loaded on board a vessel.
A foreign supplier understandably wants the right to terminate when things go badly. I have seen draft agreements that allow termination for any reason on 90 days’ notice, even though the distributor is expected to spend heavily developing the brand. Ask yourself why a serious distributor would agree to invest in a market it can lose after three months’ notice. When a prospective distributor accepts those terms without a murmur, or never asks for automatic renewal once it hits its targets, I get suspicious about how much money it actually intends to spend. The contract term ought to reflect the product and the investment required. We start some relationships with a trial period and others with a longer term and regular purchase targets.
Unlike the law in some other countries, Chinese law generally does not give ordinary distributors a special statutory right to goodwill compensation simply because a distribution agreement ends. A foreign supplier that terminates in breach of its contract still faces a damages claim. A clause allowing termination for “breach” without specifying the grounds, notice requirements, or cure procedures leaves plenty to fight about when the parties disagree over what went wrong.
I distrust China contracts that read beautifully in English and provide for a lawsuit thousands of miles from the distributor’s assets. For a mainland Chinese distributor, we ordinarily choose Chinese law and Chinese courts. Nearly all of our China contracts are bilingual, with Chinese as the controlling language. We never make both languages equally authoritative, because that invites an avoidable fight over what the parties agreed to.
When the defendant and its assets are in China, Chinese courts are generally the more direct and less expensive choice. I also think highly of CIETAC arbitration. State-owned enterprises often insist on it, and I prefer it when the distributor is in a smaller city where the local court is a concern. With CIETAC, freezing a distributor’s assets still requires a Chinese court. We tend to leave the dispute-resolution provision until late in the drafting, and sometimes have two to five of our lawyers discuss jurisdiction and governing law before settling on it.
An English trading name and an informal signature do not establish which Chinese legal entity agreed to the deal. The agreement needs the distributor’s correct registered Chinese legal name, and we normally also require its official company seal, or chop.
If a distributor registers our client’s brand, sells outside its agreed territory, or keeps using the trademark after termination, our client needs a contract that clearly prohibits that conduct and provides a remedy that works under Chinese law. We frequently include contract damages provisions for those breaches. Those provisions can help define the monetary claim and support an application for property preservation, including a bank-account freeze. A damages clause does not freeze assets by itself. The court decides whether to grant preservation and can require security. Chinese companies generally understand what a damages clause can lead to in their own courts, which makes it one of the best tools we have for getting them to honor the contract. Pages of broad American-style indemnification language will not cure a contract that lacks usable remedies under Chinese law.
When a distribution relationship ends, the distributor is still holding whatever it has not sold. Without an agreed procedure, the parties fight over whether the distributor can sell the remaining inventory, whether the supplier must buy it back, and at what price. We answer those questions in the agreement, along with pending orders and continuing warranty obligations, while the two sides are still on speaking terms.
The foreign supplier needs some of the distributor’s customer information to keep selling in China, even if the distributor built those customer relationships. Where those records contain personal information, China’s Personal Information Protection Law governs how they are handled and when they can be sent outside China. The agreement must account for those limits instead of promising an unrestricted transfer. We establish who controls the Chinese websites, e-commerce storefronts, social media accounts, and domain names used to sell the brand. If a product approval cannot legally or practically be transferred, the contract needs realistic cooperation obligations rather than a meaningless promise to hand everything over.

At the very least, get your application on file first, though a pending application is not the equivalent of an issued registration. Choose your Chinese-language brand name yourself. If you leave that decision entirely to your distributor or the market, Chinese customers can end up knowing your product by a name someone else picked. Our China trademark registration guide explains the filing process, and China Trademarks and Your Chinese Distributor covers what a distributor can do to you by filing first.

We give the distributor only the trademark rights it needs to market and sell our client’s products. Those rights end with the distribution agreement, subject to any agreed inventory sell-off rights. The distributor may not register the client’s marks, Chinese names, logos, domains, or confusingly similar brands. Where a registered mark is licensed, we address recordal of the license with the Chinese trademark authorities. An unrecorded license is generally valid between the parties but cannot be asserted against good-faith third parties. If the distributor will receive valuable confidential information, we consider the protections in our China NNN agreement guide.

3. Do Not Let Chinese Product Approvals Trap You

Before granting distribution rights, we check whether the product needs testing, certification, registration, Chinese labeling, or import permits. The agreement says who obtains and pays for each approval. If the distributor is responsible, we set a deadline and specify the consequences for missing it. Without that, a foreign supplier can wait indefinitely for sales that cannot legally begin.

I always want to know whose name will appear on each approval. An American medical device company we represented let its Chinese distributor act as its registration agent because the distributor offered to handle the paperwork at no charge. Five years later, the company wanted a stronger distributor. The old one was sitting on the registration certificate and the technical file and had no reason to cooperate. Every month it stalled was a month without sales. Where Chinese rules allow, we usually want the registration in our client’s name.

The agreement specifies who handles warranty service and pays for recalls, including whether the supplier warrants directly to end customers or only to the distributor. Those provisions do not automatically shield the manufacturer from Chinese product-liability claims. If the distributor has few assets and inadequate insurance, its promise to indemnify the manufacturer is not worth much after a major product problem.

4. I Am Wary of Nationwide Exclusivity

Chinese distributors often ask for nationwide exclusivity. A distributor that knows the Shanghai market well does not necessarily have useful contacts in Chengdu or Guangzhou, and I rarely like granting rights to all of China without a strong business reason. We define the territory, products, and customers the distributor’s rights cover, and whether our client keeps the right to sell directly or appoint other distributors.

We have seen companies sign five-year exclusive agreements and learn, two or three years in, that the distributor never placed a single order. The distributor signed to keep the product off the market while selling its own competing line, a pattern I describe in International Distribution Agreements: Beware the Eager Distributor. When our clients do grant exclusivity, we normally attach minimum purchase requirements, because purchases show up on invoices and claimed retail sales are much harder to verify. The agreement defines how performance is measured, any cure period, and the consequences of missing a target. During the exclusive period, we generally bar the distributor from handling competing products, after checking that restriction against the competition law that applies.

I like to give the supplier the right to end exclusivity without terminating the agreement. Suppose a distributor is selling a reasonable amount in Shanghai but nowhere near enough to justify control over all of China. Our client can appoint another distributor for the uncovered market and keep the Shanghai relationship if it still makes commercial sense.

5. Chinese Competition Law Limits Resale Price Controls

Clients worried about heavy discounting sometimes want to require their Chinese distributors to maintain minimum resale prices. We examine Chinese antitrust law before putting such restrictions in a contract. Article 18 of China’s Anti-Monopoly Law restricts agreements that fix resale prices or set minimum resale prices. China’s rules effective February 1, 2026 provide only a narrow safe harbor for certain fixed or minimum resale-price restrictions. In general, the party relying on the safe harbor has to prove that each party had less than a 5% share of its respective relevant market in every year of the agreement and that annual turnover of the covered goods stayed below RMB 100 million. Where the supplier has multiple distributors, their market shares in the same relevant market and the turnover of the covered goods are aggregated. Even if those thresholds are met, the safe harbor does not apply where evidence shows the agreement eliminates or restricts competition.

For most clients, we focus on the supplier’s wholesale price and let the distributor determine its own resale prices. None of our clients has ever had a real resale-price problem in China, but a number of distributors have threatened to sue our clients or report them to the authorities when relationships turned rocky, claiming minimum prices our clients never imposed. The agreements contained no price restrictions to support those threats. When resale price control matters to the business, we review the specific restriction and the law that applies before anyone signs. Form contracts imported from other countries cause enough trouble that we do not rely on whatever price clause the client’s standard agreement contains.

6. Settle the Marketing Budget Before Signing

I keep seeing the same fight start before a single order is placed. The supplier assumes the distributor will pay for advertising in exchange for exclusivity. The distributor expects the supplier to fund trade shows and provide samples, translations, and technical support. Nobody has worked out a budget. Six months later, both sides are annoyed, and sales have barely begun.

We try to settle who pays for what before we start drafting. If the distributor promises to translate manuals by a deadline or demonstrate the product to specified customers, we put those obligations in the agreement, along with our client’s marketing commitments. A general promise to “promote the brand” is useless when the first year’s sales come in far below expectations.

7. Get Paid and Get the Shipping Terms Right

For a new distributor, I favor payment before shipment. After I wrote about selling into China without being there, two clients emailed me with the same advice. However you structure the deal, get paid enough up front to make it worth your while, because there is a very good chance you will never see another cent. Once the distributor establishes a payment history, a client may decide to offer 30-day terms. If it does, the agreement needs a way to return to advance payment when the distributor pays late or its finances deteriorate. We often put prices in a separate schedule, with a defined procedure for updating them, rather than locking prices into a long-term contract.

Shipping terms create avoidable disputes when the parties use familiar acronyms without understanding what they require, so identify the Incoterms rule and the named place. For many shipments, FCA (Free Carrier) makes more sense than EXW (Ex Works), which puts export clearance on the buyer even when that buyer is in China. For containerized freight, CIP (Carriage and Insurance Paid To) often fits better than CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight), which was designed for goods loaded on board a vessel.

8. A Good Distributor Needs Time to Build the Market

A foreign supplier understandably wants the right to terminate when things go badly. I have seen draft agreements that allow termination for any reason on 90 days’ notice, even though the distributor is expected to spend heavily developing the brand. Ask yourself why a serious distributor would agree to invest in a market it can lose after three months’ notice. When a prospective distributor accepts those terms without a murmur, or never asks for automatic renewal once it hits its targets, I get suspicious about how much money it actually intends to spend. The contract term ought to reflect the product and the investment required. We start some relationships with a trial period and others with a longer term and regular purchase targets.

Unlike the law in some other countries, Chinese law generally does not give ordinary distributors a special statutory right to goodwill compensation simply because a distribution agreement ends. A foreign supplier that terminates in breach of its contract still faces a damages claim. A clause allowing termination for “breach” without specifying the grounds, notice requirements, or cure procedures leaves plenty to fight about when the parties disagree over what went wrong.

9. Draft for Enforcement Against a Chinese Company

I distrust China contracts that read beautifully in English and provide for a lawsuit thousands of miles from the distributor’s assets. For a mainland Chinese distributor, we ordinarily choose Chinese law and Chinese courts. Nearly all of our China contracts are bilingual, with Chinese as the controlling language. We never make both languages equally authoritative, because that invites an avoidable fight over what the parties agreed to.

When the defendant and its assets are in China, Chinese courts are generally the more direct and less expensive choice. I also think highly of CIETAC arbitration. State-owned enterprises often insist on it, and I prefer it when the distributor is in a smaller city where the local court is a concern. With CIETAC, freezing a distributor’s assets still requires a Chinese court. We tend to leave the dispute-resolution provision until late in the drafting, and sometimes have two to five of our lawyers discuss jurisdiction and governing law before settling on it.

An English trading name and an informal signature do not establish which Chinese legal entity agreed to the deal. The agreement needs the distributor’s correct registered Chinese legal name, and we normally also require its official company seal, or chop.

If a distributor registers our client’s brand, sells outside its agreed territory, or keeps using the trademark after termination, our client needs a contract that clearly prohibits that conduct and provides a remedy that works under Chinese law. We frequently include contract damages provisions for those breaches. Those provisions can help define the monetary claim and support an application for property preservation, including a bank-account freeze. A damages clause does not freeze assets by itself. The court decides whether to grant preservation and can require security. Chinese companies generally understand what a damages clause can lead to in their own courts, which makes it one of the best tools we have for getting them to honor the contract. Pages of broad American-style indemnification language will not cure a contract that lacks usable remedies under Chinese law.

10. Plan the Breakup While the Relationship Is Still Good

When a distribution relationship ends, the distributor is still holding whatever it has not sold. Without an agreed procedure, the parties fight over whether the distributor can sell the remaining inventory, whether the supplier must buy it back, and at what price. We answer those questions in the agreement, along with pending orders and continuing warranty obligations, while the two sides are still on speaking terms.

The foreign supplier needs some of the distributor’s customer information to keep selling in China, even if the distributor built those customer relationships. Where those records contain personal information, China’s Personal Information Protection Law governs how they are handled and when they can be sent outside China. The agreement must account for those limits instead of promising an unrestricted transfer. We establish who controls the Chinese websites, e-commerce storefronts, social media accounts, and domain names used to sell the brand. If a product approval cannot legally or practically be transferred, the contract needs realistic cooperation obligations rather than a meaningless promise to hand everything over.
